Chapter 1 — Fundamental Concepts, Addition Compounds and Oxidation States

Coordination Chemistry

Double salt

They are formed by chemical combination of two or more salts in fixed proportion.

KCl + MgCl2 + 6H2O  →  KCl·MgCl2·6H2O

(n = 5 ions: K+, Mg2+, 3Cl−)

They give test of all constituent ions in aq. solution.

KCl·MgCl2·6H2O – gives test of K+, Mg2+ and Cl−.

They lose their own identity but do not lose identity of constituent ions.

K2SO4·Al2(SO4)3·24H2O H2O⟶  2K+ + 2Al3+ + 4SO42−

Potash alum (n = 8)

(NH4)2SO4·FeSO4·6H2O H2O⟶  2NH4+ + Fe2+ + 2SO42−

Mohr salt (FAS)

Tutton's salt – M2SO4·CuSO4·6H2O (M = Na or K)

Chrome alum – K2SO4·Cr2(SO4)3·24H2O

Alum

M2SO4·M′2(SO4)3·24H2O

M = monovalent (Na+, K+, Tl+, NH4+ … etc.)

M′ = trivalent (Al3+, Fe3+, Cr3+ … etc.)

(a) If the trivalent cation is Al, the name will be according to the monovalent cation.

K2SO4·Al2(SO4)3·24H2OPotash alum
(NH4)2SO4·Al2(SO4)3·24H2OAmmonium alum

(b) If the trivalent cation is not Al, the name will be according to the trivalent cation.

K2SO4·Fe2(SO4)3·24H2OFerric alum
K2SO4·Cr2(SO4)3·24H2OChrome alum

Pseudo alum – M2SO4·M′SO4·24H2O

M′ = divalent cation (Zn2+ … etc.) (e.g. K2SO4·ZnSO4·24H2O)

→ Li+ does not form alum.

Li+ = 1s2 2s0 2p0

K2SO4·Al2(SO4)3·24H2O water⟶  2[K(H2O)6]+ + 2[Al(H2O)6]3+ + 4SO42−

Complex salt

Molecular addition compound which does not give test of all of its constituent ions in aqueous solution. They do not lose their identity but the constituent ions lose their identity.

K4[FeII(CN)6] H2O⟶  4K+ + [Fe(CN)6]4−

K3[FeIII(CN)6] H2O⟶  3K+ + [Fe(CN)6]3−

(a)

2KCN + FeSO4  →  Fe(CN)2 + K2SO4

4KCN + Fe(CN)2  →  K4[Fe(CN)6]

(b)

KCN + AgCN  →  K[Ag(CN)2]

K[Ag(CN)2]  →  K+ + [Ag(CN)2]−

(c)

2KCN·M(CN)2  →  K2[M(CN)4]

K2[M(CN)4]  →  2K+ + [M(CN)4]2−

(e)

K3[Co(NO2)6]  →  3K+ + [Co(NO2)6]3−

[Co(NH3)6]Cl3  →  [Co(NH3)6]3+ + 3Cl−

Types of co-ordination compounds

(a) On the basis of charge

(1) Anionic complex – K4[Fe(CN)6], [Co(NO2)6]3−, K2[PtCl6], etc.

(2) Cationic complex – [Cr(NH3)6]3+, [Cu(H2O)4]SO4·H2O etc.

[Cu(H2O)4]SO4·H2O = blue vitriol, C.N. = 4

(3) Neutral complex – [Ni0(CO)4], [Fe0(CO)5], [CrIII(NH3)3Cl3] etc.

(4) Complex cation – complex anion salt

[CrIII(NH3)6]3+[CoIIICl6]3−

(b) On the basis of types of ligand

(i) Homoleptic complex – only one type of ligand: [Cr(NH3)6]3+, [Ni(CO)4](ii) Heteroleptic complex – more than one type of ligand: [Cr(NH3)3Cl3]

(c) On the basis of degree of dissociation (DOD)

It is of two types:

(i) Perfect complex or penetrating complex

(ii) Imperfect complex or normal complex

Perfect complexImperfect complex
negligible DODhigh DOD
[Fe(CN)6]3−  ⇌  Fe3+ + 6CN− (negligible dissociation)[Cd(CN)4]2−  ⇌  Cd2+ + 4CN− (high DOD)
(1) [Fe(CN)6]3− + SCN−  →  no blood red colouration. It is perfect w.r.t. SCN− (Fe(SCN)3 – blood red)(1) [Cd(CN)4]2− + H2S  →  CdS (yellow). It is imperfect w.r.t. H2S
(2) [Cu(CN)4]3− + H2S  →  no ppt. It is perfect w.r.t. H2S (CuS → black)(2) [FeF6]3− (colourless) + 3OH−  →  Fe(OH)3↓ (brown) + 6F−. It is imperfect w.r.t. OH−

Terms related to co-ordination compounds

(1) Central metal atom – It is the metal which forms co-ordinate or dative bond with ligands by accepting e− pair. They act as Lewis acid.

e.g. [Cu(NH3)4]2+

Complexes may have more than one central metal.

(2) Co-ordination sphere – the central metal atom together with the ligands directly attached to it, written inside the square brackets [ ].

(3) Ionisation sphere – the counter-ions written outside the square brackets; they dissociate in water and give their usual tests.

(4) Oxidation state – the charge the central metal would carry if all ligands were removed together with the electron pairs they share with it.

(5) Co-ordination number – It is equal to the number of dative bonds formed between metal and ligands.

(6) Co-ordination polyhedra – [Cr(NH3)6]3+

(b) C3H5−

(c) η6−C6H6: 6e−

(d) η4−C4H6: 4e−

(3) K2[Cr(NH3)(CN)2(O)2(O2)] (ligands: CN−, (O2−)2, O22−)

Why Li+ does not form an alum

Alums need a large monovalent cation in the lattice. Li+ is very small with a very high charge density and normally binds only four water molecules ([Li(H2O)4]+), so it does not fit the alum structure.

Chapter 2 — Classification of Ligands, Chelation, HSAB and Hapticity

(7) Ligands – They are atoms/molecules/ions which form co-ordinate bond with metal by donating e− pair. They are Lewis bases.

They may be neutral, –vely charged or +vely charged.

Classification of ligands

(1) On the basis of charge

(a) Neutral ligand – CO, NO, PR3, PPh3, NH3, H2O, C6H6, C2H4, pyridine, NH2–CH2CH2–NH2, RNH2, PH3 etc.

(b) Negatively charged ligand – F−, Cl−, Br−, OH−, SO42−, CH3−, H−, PO43−, ClO3−, CN− etc.

(c) Positively charged ligand – NO+, N2H5+, H3O+, C6H5NH3+ etc.

No. of O–Co–O bonds = 6

Uses of EDTA

1. For removal of lead poison.

Pb2+ + CaEDTA  →  [Pb(EDTA)]2− + Ca2+

[Pb(EDTA)]²⁻ is soluble in water

2. It is used to remove hardness of water.

3. EDTA is used for estimation of Ca and Mg in basic medium. In acidic medium EDTA gets protonated.

Q. Which of the following does not form complex with EDTA?

(a) Be2+ (b) Ca2+ (c) Sr2+ (d) Ba2+

Ans. (a) Be2+

Reason: Be2+ is a second-period ion with a maximum co-ordination number of 4, so it cannot be bound by hexadentate EDTA (which needs C.N. 6); the other three ions can.

Chelating agent

When a polydentate ligand attaches to the central metal through two or more donor atoms, a ring type closed structure is produced; this phenomenon is called chelation and the ligands are called chelating ligands.

e.g. bi-, tri-, tetra- … dentate ligands.

Ambidentate ligands

When a ligand contains two or more types of donor atom, but at the time of co-ordination only one can co-ordinate, such ligands are called ambidentate ligands.

(a)–C≡N− (bound through C)cyano
–N≡C (bound through N)isocyano
(b)–O–C≡Ncyanato or cyanato-O
–N=C=Oisocyanato or cyanato-N

–N=C=Sisothiocyanato or thiocyanato-N
(d)–NO2nitro or nitrito-N

In thiosulphate the central S has oxidation state +6 and the terminal S has –2.

(g) –SeCN: selenocyanato-Se; –NCSe: selenocyanato-N

(i) Sulphoxide: –O–SR2 (O-bonded) and –S(=O)R2 (S-bonded)

Different factors which determine the binding site of an ambidentate ligand which will participate to co-ordinate are –

(i) hard–soft character

(ii) steric crowding

(iii) π-bonding properties

(iv) pH of the solution

[Hg(SCN)4]2−: Hg2+ prefers S; all 4 SCN ligands co-ordinate with Hg2+ through S.

Fe4[Fe(CN)6]3 ← misleading formula: Fe3+ is not in the ionisation sphere.

The formula is FeII3FeIII4(CN)18.

It is written this way as made from the reaction:

4Fe3+ + 3[Fe(CN)6]4−  →  Fe4[Fe(CN)6]3

Different oxidation states have different preference:

Fe3+ – hard acid – prefers N

Fe2+ – soft acid – prefers C

Iron-cyanido complex: (i) The iron-cyanido complexes are of much importance in this regard. Prussian blue, Turnbull's blue and other related compounds have similar structures.

K+ + Fe2+ + [Fe(CN)6]3−  →  Turnbull's blue

K+ + Fe3+ + [Fe(CN)6]4−  →  Prussian blue

Both the blues have the similar bridged network structure having the –FeII–C≡N–FeIII segments. FeII– and FeIII– centres are positioned at the corners of the cubes. The cubes are stacked to produce the cubic lattice where the requisite amount of K+ ions occupy the centres of alternate cubes to give the composition KFeFe(CN)6. Water molecules may also occupy the cubic holes. Thus, Prussian blue and other related materials adopt the three dimensional polymeric structure.

Unit cube of polymeric Prussian blue KFeIIFeIII(CN)6: FeII and FeIII alternate at the 8 corners, a C≡N bridge lies on each of the 12 edges (K+ ions sit in alternate cubes)

In Prussian blue, the starting material possesses the FeII–CN linkage while in Turnbull's blue the starting material bears the FeIII–CN linkage. Thus it is reasonable to assume that in Prussian blue it should have the linkage –FeII–C≡N–FeIII– while Turnbull's blue should contain the linkage –FeIII–C≡N–FeII–. But the linkage –FeII–C≡N–FeIII– is stabler than the –FeIII–C≡N–FeII– linkage. In 'C≡N', the C-end is a strong field ligand which can generate a high CFSE (crystal field stabilization energy) for the FeII (d6) – low spin complex (t2g6). The N-end is a relatively weak field ligand that forms a high-spin complex with the FeIII centre (t2g3 eg2) which is resistant to some extent to spin pairing due to the high exchange energy. Besides these, the softer C-end matches better with the Fe(II) centre while the relatively harder N-end matches better with the relatively harder Fe(III) centre. Thus, the C-end preferably links with the FeII centre. The linkage –FeIII–C≡N–FeII– initially present in Turnbull's blue isomerizes slowly to the –FeII–C≡N–FeIII– linkage which is thermodynamically stabler.

Imp. SnCl3− is a monodentate ligand (trichlorostannato), bonded through Sn.

η-Nomenclature for ligands

In organometallic chemistry in particular, but also in co-ordination chemistry, use of the Greek prefix η (eta) is encountered; the letter is accompanied by a superscript number (e.g. η3). This prefix describes the number of atoms in a ligand which directly interact with the metal centre, the hapticity of the ligand. For example, the cyclopentadienyl ligand, [C5H5]− or Cp−, is versatile in its modes of bonding, and examples include those shown below. Note the different ways of representing the η3− and η5−modes. In co-ordination chemistry, the η terminology is used for ligands such as [O2]2− (peroxido ligand).

Hapticity

It is defined as the co-ordination of a ligand with the central metal atom via an uninterrupted and contiguous series of atoms.

For π-donor ligands, the word hapticity is used (not denticity).

It is represented by the Greek letter η (eta).

NO → NO+ nitrosylium: 2e−

NO → NO nitrosyl (NO+ + e−): 3e−

[Cr(H2O)3(NO)2]: EAN = 36 in both cases of NO and NO+

IntermediateBr−, [N3]−, py, [SCN]− (N-bound), ArNH2, [NO2]−, [SO3]2−Pb2+, Fe2+, Co2+, Ni2+, Cu2+, Os2+, Ru3+, Rh3+, Ir3+

1. O donors are generally WFL but act as SFL for Co3+ and Cu2+.

2. Generally NH3 is SFL but acts as WFL for Mn2+, Fe2+.

3. All ligands are SFL for the 4d and 5d series.

Chapter 3 — Coordination Number and Coordination Polyhedra

Co-ordination number 2

Examples of co-ordination number 2 are uncommon, being generally restricted to Cu(I), Ag(I), Au(I) and Hg(II), all d10 ions. Examples include [CuCl2]−, [Ag(NH3)2]+, [Au(CN)2]−, (R3P)AuCl, [Au(PR3)2]+ (R = alkyl or aryl) and Hg(CN)2, in each of which the metal centre is in a linear environment. However, in the solid state, the Cu(I) centre in K[Cu(CN)2] is 3-co-ordinate by virtue of cyanido-bridge formation. Bulky amido ligands, e.g. [N(SiR3)2]−, are often associated with low co-ordination numbers. For example, in [Fe{N(SiMePh2)2}2] (∠N–Fe–N = 169°), the sterically demanding amido groups force a 2-co-ordinate environment on a metal centre that usually prefers to be surrounded by a greater number of ligands.

Co-ordination number 3

3-Co-ordinate complexes are not common. Usually, trigonal planar structures are observed, and examples involving d10 metal centres include:

• Cu(I) in [Cu(CN)3]2−, [Cu(CN)2]− (see above), [Cu(SPMe3)3]+;

• Ag(I) in [AgTe7]3−, [Ag(PPh3)3]+;

• Au(I) in [Au{PPh(C6H11)2}3]+;

• Hg(II) in [HgI3]−, [Hg(SPh)3]−;

• Pt(0) in [Pt(PPh3)3], [Pt(PtBu2H)3].

Sterically demanding amido ligands have been used to stabilize complexes containing 3-co-ordinate metal ions, e.g. [Fe{N(SiMe3)2}3]. In the solid state, [Y{N(SiMe3)2}3] and [Sc{N(SiMe3)2}3] possess trigonal pyramidal metal centres (∠N–Y–N = 115° and ∠N–Sc–N = 115.5°), but it is likely that crystal packing effects cause the deviation from planarity. The fact that in the gas phase [Sc{N(SiMe3)2}3] contains a trigonal planar Sc(III) centre supports this proposal.

p-Block chemistry has a number of examples of T-shaped molecules (e.g. ClF3) in which stereochemically active lone pairs play a crucial role. d-Block metal complexes do not mimic this behaviour, although ligand constraints (e.g. the bite angle of a chelate) may distort a 3-co-ordinate structure away from the expected trigonal planar structure.

Co-ordination number 4

4-Co-ordinate complexes are extremely common, with a tetrahedral arrangement of donor atoms being the most frequently observed. The tetrahedron is sometimes 'flattened', distortions being attributed to steric or crystal packing effects or, in some cases, electronic effects. Tetrahedral complexes for d3 ions are rarely, if ever, encountered. The complex drawn below exemplifies the stabilization of 4-co-ordinate Cr3+ (d3) using a tripodal ligand. This co-ordination geometry is enforced by the ligand, and the Cr–N distances in the 'trigonal plane' are shorter (188 pm) than the axial distance (224 pm).

Cr(III) held by the tripodal amido ligand N(CH₂CH₂NSiMe₃)₃³⁻ (three NSiMe₃ in the trigonal plane, amine N axial; the three arms link the axial N to each NSiMe₃)

Tetrahedral complexes for d4 ions have been stabilized only with bulky amido ligands, e.g. [M(NPh2)4] and [M{N(SiMe3)2}3Cl] for M = Hf or Zr. Simple tetrahedral species include:

• d0: [VO4]3−, [CrO4]2−, [MoS4]2−, [WS4]2−, [MnO4]−, [TcO4]−, RuO4, OsO4;

• d1: [MnO4]2−, [TcO4]2−, [ReO4]2−, [RuO4]−;

• d2: [FeO4]2−, [RuO4]2−;

• d5: [FeCl4]−, [MnCl4]2−;

• d6: [FeCl4]2−, [FeI4]2−;

• d7: [CoCl4]2−;

• d8: [NiCl4]2−, [NiBr4]2−;

• d9: [CuCl4]2− (distorted);

• d10: [ZnCl4]2−, [HgBr4]2−, [CdCl4]2−, [Zn(OH)4]2−, [Cu(CN)4]3−, [Ni(CO)4].

The solid state structures of apparently simple anions may in fact be polymeric (e.g. the presence of fluoride bridges in [CoF4]2− and [NiF4]2− leads to a layered structure with octahedral metal centres) or may be cation-dependent (e.g. discrete tetrahedral [MnCl4]2− ions are present in the Cs+ and [Me4N]+ salts, but a polymeric structure with Mn–Cl–Mn bridges is adopted by the Na+ salt).

Square planar complexes are rarer than tetrahedral, and are often associated with d8 configurations where electronic factors strongly favour a square planar arrangement, e.g. [PdCl4]2−, [PtCl4]2−, [AuCl4]−, [AuBr4]−, [RhCl(PPh3)3] and trans-[IrCl(CO)(PPh3)2]. The classification of distorted structures such as those in [Ir(PMePh2)4]+ and [Rh(PMe2Ph)4]+ may be ambiguous, but in this case, the fact that each metal ion is d8 suggests that steric crowding causes deviation from a square planar arrangement (not from a tetrahedral one). The [Co(CN)4]2− ion is a rare example of a square planar d7 complex.

Co-ordination number 5

The limiting structures for 5-co-ordination are the trigonal bipyramid and square-based pyramid. In practice, many structures lie between these two extremes, the energy difference between trigonal bipyramidal and square-based pyramidal structures usually being small. Among simple 5-co-ordinate complexes are trigonal bipyramidal [CdCl5]3−, [HgCl5]3− (d10) and [CuCl5]3− (d9) and a series of square-based pyramidal oxido- or nitrido-complexes in which the oxido or nitrido ligand occupies the axial site:

• d0: [NbCl4(O)]−;

• d1: [V(acac)2(O)], [WCl4(O)]−, [TcCl4(N)]−, [TcBr4(N)]−;

• d2: [TcCl4(O)]−, [ReCl4(O)]−.

[WCl4(O)]− (left) and [TcCl4(N)]− (right)

The formulae of some complexes may misleadingly suggest '5-co-ordinate' metal centres: e.g. Cs3CoCl5 is actually Cs3[CoCl4]Cl.

5-Co-ordinate structures are found for many compounds with polydentate amine, phosphane or arsane ligands. Of particular interest among these are complexes containing tripodal ligands in which the central atom is a donor atom. This makes the ligand ideally suited to occupy one axial and the three equatorial sites of a trigonal bipyramidal complex as in [CoBr{N(CH2CH2NMe2)3}]+, [Rh(SH){P(CH2CH2PPh2)3}] and [Zn{N(CH2CH2NH2)3}Cl]+. On the other

Examples of 4- and 5-co-ordinate structures (X-ray data): (a) [Rh(PMe2Ph)4]+ – steric demands of the ligands distort the structure from the square planar structure expected for this d8 metal centre; (b) [Zn{N(CH2CH2NH2)3}Cl]+ – trigonal bipyramidal; (c) [Cu(bpy){NH(CH2CO2)2}] (crystallized as the hexahydrate) – square-based pyramidal

hand, the conformational constraints of the ligands may result in a preference for a square-based pyramidal complex in the solid state, e.g. [Cu(bpy){NH(CH2CO2)2}]·6H2O.

Co-ordination number 6

For many years after Werner's proof from stereochemical studies that many 6-co-ordinate complexes of chromium and cobalt had octahedral structures, it was believed that no other form of 6-co-ordination occurred, and a vast amount of data from X-ray diffraction studies seemed to support this. Eventually, however, examples of trigonal prismatic co-ordination were confirmed.

The regular or nearly regular octahedral co-ordination sphere is found for all electronic configurations from d0 to d10, e.g. [TiF6]2− (d0), [Ti(OH2)6]3+ (d1), [V(OH2)6]3+ (d2), [Cr(OH2)6]3+ (d3), [Mn(OH2)6]3+ (d4), [Fe(OH2)6]3+ (d5), [Fe(OH2)6]2+ (d6), [Co(OH2)6]2+ (d7), [Ni(OH2)6]2+ (d8), [Cu(NO2)6]4− (d9) and [Zn(OH2)6]2+ (d10). There are distinctions between what are termed low-spin and high-spin complexes: where the distinction is meaningful, the examples listed above are high-spin complexes, but many octahedral low-spin complexes are also known, e.g. [Mn(CN)6]3− (d4), [Fe(CN)6]3− (d5), [Co(CN)6]3− (d6). Octahedral complexes of d4 and d9 metal ions tend to be tetragonally distorted, i.e. they are elongated or squashed. This is an electronic effect called Jahn–Teller distortion.

While the vast majority of 6-co-ordinate complexes containing simple ligands are octahedral, there is a small group of d0 or d1 metal complexes in which the metal centre is in a trigonal prismatic or distorted trigonal prismatic environment. The octahedron and trigonal prism are closely related, and can be described in terms of two triangles which are staggered (octahedron) or eclipsed (trigonal prism).

The complexes [ReMe6] (d1), [TaMe6]− (d0) and [ZrMe6]2− (d0) contain regular trigonal prismatic (D3h) metal centres, while in [MoMe6] (d0), [WMe6] (d0), [NbMe6]− (d0) and [TaPh6]− (d0) the co-ordination environment is distorted trigonal prismatic (C3v). The common feature of the ligands in these complexes is that they are σ-donors, with no π-donating or π-accepting properties. In [Li(TMEDA)]2[Zr(SC6H4–4–Me)6] (TMEDA = Me2NCH2CH2NMe2), the [Zr(SC6H4–4–Me)6]2− ion also has a distorted trigonal prismatic structure. Although thiolate ligands are usually weak π-donor ligands, it has been suggested that the cation–anion interactions in crystalline [Li(TMEDA)]2[Zr(SC6H4–4–Me)6] result in the RS− ligands behaving only as σ-donors. Another related group of trigonal prismatic d0, d1 or d2 metal complexes contains

The trigonal prismatic structures of (a) [WMe6] and (b) [Re(S2C2Ph2)3] (each S–S edge of the prism belongs to one dithiolate ligand)

the dithiolate ligands (structure below) and includes [Mo(S2C2H2)3] and [Re(S2C2Ph2)3].

The complexes [WL3], [TiL3]2−, [ZrL3]2− and [HfL3]2− (L = ligand drawn below) also possess trigonal prismatic structures. For a regular trigonal prism, the twist angle α (angle between the upper and lower triangular faces viewed down the 3-fold axis) is 0° and this is observed for [TiL3]2− and [HfL3]2−. In [ZrL3]2−, α = 3°, and in [WL3], α = 15°. Formally, [WL3] contains W(0) and is a d6 complex, while [ML3]2− (M = Ti, Zr, Hf) contains the metal in a –2 oxidation state. However, theoretical results for [WL3] indicate that negative charge is transferred on to the ligands. In the extreme case, the ligands can be formulated as L2− and the metal as a d0 centre.

(a) [Mn(acac)2(bpy)] – trigonal prismatic; (b) [Mn(acac)2(phen)] – octahedral

The solid state structures of [Mn(acac)2(bpy)] (trigonal prismatic) and [Mn(acac)2(phen)] (octahedral) provide an example in which crystal packing forces appear to dictate the difference in ligand arrangement. The energy difference between the two structures is calculated to be very small, and the preference for a trigonal prism in [Mn(acac)2(bpy)] is observed only in the solid state.

Co-ordination number 7

High co-ordination numbers (≥7) are observed most frequently for ions of the early second and third row d-block metals and for the lanthanoids and actinoids, i.e. rcation must be relatively large. The arrangement of the donor atoms for the three idealized 7-co-ordinate structures is: pentagonal bipyramid, monocapped octahedron and monocapped trigonal prism. In the capped trigonal prism, the 'cap' is over one of the square faces of the prism. In reality, there is much distortion from these idealized structures, and this is apparent for the example of a capped octahedral complex. The anions in [Li(OEt2)]+[MoMe7]− and [Li(OEt2)]+[WMe7]− are further examples of capped octahedral structures. A problem in the chemical literature is that the distortions may lead to ambiguity in the way in which a given structure is described. Among binary metal halides and pseudohalides, 7-co-ordinate structures are exemplified by the pentagonal bipyramidal ions [V(CN)7]4− (d2) and [NbF7]3− (d1). In the ammonium salt, [ZrF7]3− (d0) is pentagonal bipyramidal, but in the guanidinium salt, it has a monocapped trigonal prismatic structure. Further examples of monocapped trigonal prismatic complexes are [NbF7]2− and [TaF7]2− (d0). 7-Co-ordinate complexes containing oxido ligands may favour pentagonal bipyramidal structures with the oxido group in an axial site, e.g. [Nb(O)(ox)3]3−,

Co-ordination spheres defined by the donor atoms in idealized 7-co-ordinate structures. Examples (X-ray data): capped octahedral [TaCl4(PMe3)3]; capped trigonal prismatic [ZrF7]3− in the guanidinium salt; pentagonal bipyramidal cation in [ScCl2(15–crown–5)]2[CuCl4] with the crown ether occupying the equatorial plane

[Nb(O)(OH2)2(ox)2]− and [Mo(O)(O2)2(ox)]2− (all d0). In this last example, two peroxido ligands are present, each in an η2 mode (structure below). Macrocyclic ligands containing five donor atoms (e.g. 15-crown-5) may dictate that the co-ordination geometry is pentagonal bipyramidal.

Co-ordination number 8

As the number of vertices in a polyhedron increases, so does the number of possible structures. Probably the best known 8-vertex polyhedron is the cube, but this is hardly ever observed as an arrangement of donor atoms in complexes. The few examples include the anions in the actinoid complexes Na3[PaF8], Na3[UF8] and [Et4N]4[U(NCS–N)8]. Steric hindrance between ligands can be reduced by converting a cubic into a square antiprismatic arrangement, i.e. on going from the cube (squares eclipsed) to the square antiprism (squares staggered).

cube – squares eclipsed; square antiprism – squares staggered

Square antiprismatic co-ordination environments occur in [Zr(acac)4] (d0) and in the anions in the salts Na3[TaF8] (d0), K2[ReF8] (d1) and K3[H3NCH2CH2NH3][Nb(ox)4] (d1). Specifying the counter-ion is important since the energy difference between 8-co-ordinate structures tends to be small with the result that the preference between two structures may be altered by crystal packing forces in

Co-ordination spheres defined by the donor atoms in idealized 8-co-ordinate structures (the two square faces of the square antiprism are mutually staggered). Examples (X-ray data): square antiprismatic [Nb(ox)4]4− in K3[H3NCH2CH2NH3][Nb(ox)4]·4H2O; dodecahedral [Y(OH2)8]3+ in [Y(OH2)8]Cl3·(15–crown–5); [CdBr2(18–crown–6)] with the macrocyclic ligand occupying the equatorial plane of a hexagonal bipyramid

two different salts. Examples are seen in a range of salts of [Mo(CN)8]3−, [W(CN)8]3−, [Mo(CN)8]4− or [W(CN)8]4− which possess square antiprismatic or dodecahedral structures depending on the cation. Further examples of dodecahedral complexes include [Y(OH2)8]3+ and a number of complexes with bidentate ligands: [Mo(O2)4]2− (d0), [Ti(NO3)4] (d0), [Cr(O2)4]3− (d1), [Mn(NO3)4]2− (d5) and [Fe(NO3)4]− (d5).

The hexagonal bipyramid is a rare co-ordination environment, but may be favoured in complexes containing a hexadentate macrocyclic ligand, for example [CdBr2(18–crown–6)]. A bicapped trigonal prism is another option for 8-co-ordination, but is only rarely observed, e.g. in [ZrF8]4− (d0) and [La(acac)3(OH2)2]·H2O (d0).

Co-ordination number 9

The anions [ReH9]2− and [TcH9]2− (both d0) provide examples of 9-co-ordinate species in which the metal centre is in a tricapped trigonal prismatic environment. A co-ordination number of 9 is most often associated with yttrium, lanthanum and the f-block elements. The tricapped trigonal prism is the only regular arrangement of donor atoms yet observed, e.g. in [Sc(OH2)9]3+, [Y(OH2)9]3+ and [La(OH2)9]3+.

Co-ordination numbers of 10 and above

It is always dangerous to draw conclusions on the basis of the non-existence of structure types, but, from data available at the present time, it seems that a co-ordination of ≥10 is generally confined to the f-block metal ions. Lanthanum exhibits co-ordination numbers of 10 and 12, e.g. in [La(NO3–O,O′)2(OH2)6]+ and [La(NO3–O,O′)6]3−. In both complexes, the nitrate ions are bidentate, as indicated by the nomenclature in the formulae. However, although La is in group 3, it is usually classed with the lanthanoid, rather than d-block, metals. Within the d-block, complexes containing [BH4]− and related ligands provide rare examples of co-ordination numbers >9. For example, in [Hf(BH4)4] and [Zr(MeBH3)4] the ligands are tridentate and the metal centres

(a) [La(NO3–O,O′)2(OH2)6]+ cation (CN 10: two bidentate nitrate + six aqua); (b) [Hf(BH4)4] (neutron diffraction, low temperature), each BH4− tridentate through three H atoms; (c) the 12-vertex cuboctahedral co-ordination sphere of the Hf(IV) centre in [Hf(BH4)4]

are 12-co-ordinate. The structure of [Hf(BH4)4] has a cuboctahedral arrangement of the 12 hydrogen atoms around the metal centre. The same co-ordination environment is found in [Zr(MeBH3)4].

Three-co-ordinate amido complexes

• [Fe{N(SiMe3)2}3] is trigonal planar.

• In the solid state [Y{N(SiMe3)2}3] (∠N–Y–N = 115°) and [Sc{N(SiMe3)2}3] (∠N–Sc–N = 115.5°) are slightly pyramidal because of crystal packing; gas-phase [Sc{N(SiMe3)2}3] is trigonal planar.

• d-block three-co-ordinate complexes deviate from trigonal planarity only when constrained (for example by chelate bite angles), unlike p-block T-shaped molecules such as ClF3, which owe the shape to lone pairs.

• [Ce(NO3)6]2−: C.N. = 12

• NO3− acts as a bidentate ligand.

• Till date, C.N. = 14 has been observed.

Stock number: The oxidation number (without the sign) of the metal is indicated in parentheses by the Roman numeral and Arabic zero after the name of the central metal atom (including the ending 'ate', if applicable). This is called Stock number. No space is left between the Stock number and the name of the metal.

Illustration: For the anionic complexes of trivalent chromium, bivalent nickel, bivalent palladium, trivalent cobalt, trivalent iron, the endings are chromate(III), nickelate(II), palladate(II), cobaltate(III), ferrate(III) respectively.

For the neutral and cationic complexes, the endings are like these: platinum(II), nickel(0), cobalt(III), nickel(II).

Ewens–Bassett number: It is an alternative to Stock number. The net charge of the complex is indicated by an Arabic number followed by the charge sign (called Ewens–Bassett number) within parentheses instead of the Stock number. For the neutral complex, nothing is to be added. When the oxidation number of the metal centre is ill-defined, the Ewens–Bassett number is very much useful (e.g. brown ring complex).

Names and formulae of dinuclear and polynuclear complexes with bridging ligands or metal–metal bonds

(A) Complexes with bridging ligands

• The bridging ligand is indicated by 'μ' placed before the ligand and separated by a hyphen.

• If the bridging ligand appears more than once, then the multiplicative prefixes are used, e.g. di-μ-, tri-μ-, etc.

• If the same ligand is present both as the bridging ligand and non-bridging ligand, then the bridging ligand is mentioned first followed by the corresponding non-bridging ligand, e.g. μ-chlorido-tetrachlorido…, di-μ-chloridotrichlorido….

• If a bridging ligand connects two metal centres, then it is simply represented by μ. If the ligand connects more than two metal centres, then it is denoted by μn (n > 2, denoting the number of centres connected by the bridging ligand).

(B) Complexes with metal–metal bonding

• Metal–metal bonding may be indicated separately in parentheses at the end followed by the ionic charge (i.e. Ewens–Bassett number within the parentheses). The involved metals are written by their symbols in italic fonts.

• For the symmetrical dinuclear complexes, the simpler names may be given by using the multiplicative prefixes.

• For the unsymmetrical binuclear complexes, the metal centres are numbered 1 and 2 according to a certain priority sequence and the ligating atoms are denoted by kappa as usual.

• Priority sequence of the metal centres in the unsymmetrical dinuclear complexes with the metal–metal bond: If both the metal centres are the same, the centre connected to the larger number of ligands is denoted 1 and the other is 2. If both the metal centres bear the same number of ligands, then the centre connecting the larger number of alphabetically preferred ligands is denoted by the number 1.

(C) If the metal centres are different then the more metallic centre (i.e. less electronegative) is assigned the number 1.

Formula representation of co-ordination compounds (IUPAC 2005)

Here it should be mentioned that the IUPAC-2005 recommendations differ from the earlier recommendations in many aspects. Presently, most of the books available in the market have followed the earlier recommendations. However, here we shall follow the IUPAC 2005 recommendations.

(A) Formula representation of the mononuclear complexes

(a) The order of symbols within the co-ordination formula is:

• "Central metal atom symbol followed by the ligand symbols in an alphabetical order (irrespective of their charge bearing properties)". (IUPAC 2005)

• "No space left in writing the components of a complex species".

(cf. Earlier recommendation: "Central metal atom symbol followed by the anionic ligands then by the neutral ligands; within each category of ligands, the ligands are listed in an alphabetical order".)

Alphabetical order of the ligand symbols: (i) The ligands are listed in an alphabetical order according to the first atomic symbols of their line formulae or abbreviations. (ii) If required, formulae of different ligands are ordered alphanumerically, i.e. according to the order of the atomic symbols and right subscripts to these. (iii) A single letter symbol precedes a two letter symbol with the same initial letter, e.g. CO precedes Cl. (iv) Sequence of the ligands does not depend on the charge of the ligands.

The above rules are illustrated in the following examples.

• Order of the inorganic ligands like Cl−, H2O, NH3, NO3−, SO42−, OH− is determined by the alphabetical order of the letters C, H, N, N, S, O respectively.

• For CH3CN, MeCN and NCMe (line formulae of the same substance), the order is determined by the alphabetical order of the letters C, M and N respectively.

• For H2O and OH2, they are ordered under the letters H and O respectively.

• The following N-containing ligands are ordered as: N3− (nitride), NH2−, NH3, NO2−, NO3−, N2O22− (hyponitrite), N3− (azide)

• For O2−, OH−, OH2 and NH3 the order is: NH3, O2−, OH−, OH2

Note: For formula representation, OH2 (not H2O) is used to convey the mode of ligation. If H2O and NH3 are considered, then H2O precedes NH3; but if OH2 and NH3 are considered, then NH3 precedes OH2. Thus we can write [Cr(H2O)4(NH3)2]3+ as per the earlier recommendation, but presently it is recommended as [Cr(NH3)2(OH2)4]3+.

• SCN− and NCS− are ordered under S and N respectively.

Note: It cannot be written as CNS− or SNC−.

(b) To convey more structural information by formulae, the ligand formula should be written in such a way that the donor atom symbol is written closest to the central atom symbol. This recommendation is practised when it is possible as in the case of co-ordinated water, i.e. [Ni(OH2)6]2+ but not [Ni(H2O)6]2+.

(c) Formula of a co-ordination entity (whether charged or not) is enclosed in square brackets. Formulae of the polyatomic ligands and ligand abbreviations are enclosed in parentheses.

(d) For the ionic species, cation is followed by the anion and no space is left between the representations of the cation and anion.

(e) For the charged complex species (shown without the counterion), the charge is indicated as a right hand superscript outside the enclosing square bracket [ ]. The oxidation number of the metal may be indicated by a Roman numeral placed as a right hand superscript on the elemental symbol.

(f) Isomers (e.g. cis–trans; fac–mer, etc.) and stereochemical descriptions may be indicated.

(B) Formula representation of the di- and polynuclear complexes

(a) Order of the metal centres: For the polynuclear complexes (i.e. more than one metal centre), order of the metal atoms is decided by their relative electronegativities as follows (IUPAC 2005): "the more electronegative centre comes later, i.e. the least electronegative (i.e. the most electropositive) element is listed first."

(Note: According to the earlier IUPAC recommendation, the central metal atoms are listed in an alphabetical order.)

Working rule based on the electronegativity for ordering of the central atoms: In the periodic table (having 18 groups), if we make a journey from the element F (the most electronegative one) along the conventional element-sequence path, the element which appears later is less electronegative (by convention). Thus it is concluded as follows:

"the element that appears later in the path of the arrow in traversing from F, is listed first both in the formula and name of the complex."

Illustration: Between Co and Re, Re is reached later, thus [ReCo(CO)9] is the correct formula but [CoRe(CO)9] gives the incorrect formula.

For Co and Cr, the order is CrCo. Similarly other examples of the order are: IrHg; MoRu; FeNi; CrFeCu; etc.

Note: Sometimes, to convey more structural information by a given formula, the order is relaxed, e.g. [ClHgIr(CO)Cl2(PPh3)2]. However, in naming, iridium comes before mercury.

• Additional rules are required to specify the ligand distribution around the metal centres. In the polynuclear complexes, there must be at least a bridging ligand or a direct bond between the central atoms. Bridging ligands are denoted by placing μ- before the ligand symbol. The bridging ligands are placed further away from the central atoms than the terminal ligands of the same kind, e.g. [Cr2O6(μ–O)]2−.

(b) Order of the ligands: The ligands, in general, are listed in an alphabetical order.

Chapter 5 — Classical Bonding Theories: Werner's Theory, EAN Rule and 18-Electron Rule

Werner's theory of variable valency

There are two types of valencies exhibited by a metal:

(1) Primary valency

(2) Secondary valency

Primary valencySecondary valency
1. It represents O.S.1. It represents C.N.
2. P.V. is non-directional2. S.V. is directional
3. It is satisfied by ions.3. It is satisfied by –ve, +ve and neutral ligands.
4. It is variable.4. It is fixed.
5. It may be zero.5. It cannot be zero.
6. It may be ionisable.6. It is non-ionisable.
7. P.V. is represented by dotted lines.7. It is represented by solid lines.
8. It doesn't contribute in stereochemical orientation of atoms/groups.8. It contributes in stereochemical orientation of atoms/groups.

e.g. (1) [Cr(NH3)6]Cl3: PV = 3, SV = 6

e.g. (2) [Ni(CO)4]: PV = 0, SV = 4

e.g. (3) K4[Fe(CN)6]: PV = 2, SV = 6

The two CN− groups drawn with an extra dotted line satisfy both primary and secondary valency.

e.g. (4) [Cr(NH3)3Cl3]: PV = 3, SV = 6

The three Cl− ions satisfy both primary (dotted) and secondary (solid) valency; the complex is non-ionisable.

Effective atomic number (EAN) (Sidgwick rule)

The complexes in which EAN is equal to the atomic number of the next noble gas are found to be extra stable.

EAN = atomic number of metal ± O.S. + 2 × co-ordination number

(– for positive O.S., + for negative O.S.: EAN = Z – O.S. + 2 × C.N.)

[Ni(CO)4]EAN = 28 + 0 + 2 × 4 = 36 = [Kr]
[Fe(CO)5]EAN = 26 + 10 = 36
K4[Fe(CN)6]EAN = 26 – 2 + 12 = 36
K3[Fe(CN)6]EAN = 26 – 3 + 12 = 35

If EAN is less than the atomic number of the next noble gas, then the complex undergoes reduction, dimerisation or polymerisation.

1.

[Mn(CO)5] (EAN = 35) reduction⟶  [Mn(CO)5]− (EAN = 36)

[Mn(CO)5] (EAN = 35) dimerisation⟶  [Mn2(CO)10] (EAN = 36)

[Mn(CO)5] can act as an oxidizing agent.

EAN = (2 × 25 + 10 × 2 + 2)/2 = 36

* NO donates 3e−; NO+ donates 2e−

2. [Co(CO)4]: EAN = 35

[Co(CO)4]  →  [Co(CO)4]− (reduction)

[Co(CO)4]  →  [Co2(CO)8] (dimerisation)

[Co2(CO)8] can exist in two possible tautomeric forms.

EAN = (2 × 27 + 16 + 2)/2 = 36

Limitations of the EAN rule without the structural information

When the structural information is not available, then for the polynuclear carbonyls the EAN rule cannot predict the number of bridging CO (i.e. μ2-CO) groups. It is illustrated for [Fe3(CO)12] having 3 Fe–Fe bonds. Without considering the nature of the CO groups, we have:

No. of electrons per Fe = 3 × 8 + 12 × 2 + 3 × 23 = 18

However, the actual structure is [Fe3(CO)10(μ2–CO)2] which also satisfies the 18e rule.

Here it may be noted that for the heavier congeners of iron, the corresponding trinuclear carbonyls, i.e. [Ru3(CO)12] and [Os3(CO)12], possess the structure having no bridging CO group. It is believed that for the heavier congeners (which are larger in size), the metal–metal bonds are too long to allow the bridge formation by CO. A similar situation prevails for [M4(CO)12] (M = Co, Rh, Ir) where for M = Co, Rh there are two μ2-CO groups while for M = Ir, there is no μ2-CO group. However, in each case, there are 6 M–M bonds along the edges of a tetrahedron and in each case, the EAN rule is satisfied.

The structural difference among the species [M3(CO)12] (M = Fe, Ru, Os) or [M4(CO)12] (M = Co, Rh, Ir) cannot be predicted by the EAN rule.

In this regard, [Co2(CO)8] is also relevant. In the solid state, it predominantly exists with two μ2-CO groups but in solution it may remain in equilibrium with different structural isomers. There is an isomer having no bridging CO group (i.e. all CO groups as the terminal groups). In fact, in terms of electron count, both the following structures are equivalent.

NO = 3e−; NO+ = 2e−

Fe(CO)5 2NO⟶  [Fe2−(NO)2(CO)2]

If nothing is mentioned, we take NO+ (and not NO) since NO+ is more stable than NO.

Note – NO+ is a better ligand than CO.

Application of the 18e rule

In understanding the structure and properties of metal carbonyls, the EAN rule is remarkably important. Some illustrative examples are discussed below.

• Prediction of the number of metal–metal bonds in polynuclear carbonyls: By considering the 2c–2e bond in each M–M bond, the number of such bonds can be obtained.

• Possibility of dimerization or polymerization: If the mononuclear metal carbonyls cannot attain the effective atomic number of the nearest inert gas, then the mononuclear species undergo dimerization or polymerization to attain the nearest inert gas electronic configuration.

(i) [Co(CO)4] (bearing 17 valence electrons = 9 + 4 × 2) is unstable and it dimerizes to [Co2(CO)8] to maintain the 18-electron rule.

[(OC)4Co–Co(CO)4]Co: 9e; 4CO: 4 × 2e; 1 Co–Co bond: 1e18 valence electrons around each Co-centre

It may be noted that [Co2(CO)8] can exist in two possible tautomeric structures: the all-terminal form (in hydrocarbon solvent) and [Co2(CO)6(μ2–CO)2] (in the solid state).

The structure possessing two bridging CO groups also maintains the 18e rule.

Co: 9e; 3COt: 3 × 2e; 2COb: 2 × 1e; 1 Co–Co bond: 1e = 18e18 valence electrons around each Co-centre; COt denotes the terminal CO group; COb denotes the bridging CO group

(ii) In [Mn(CO)5], the valence electron count is 17 (= 7 + 5 × 2) and to maintain the 18e rule, it undergoes dimerization to produce [Mn2(CO)10].

2[Mn(CO)5]  →  [(OC)5Mn–Mn(CO)5]

(iii) According to the EAN rule, [V(CO)6] should undergo dimerization leading to a V–V bond giving rise to [V2(CO)12]. But in fact, it does not happen. Probably, in the dimer, the steric hindrance does not favour the situation. However, it satisfies the rule in another way discussed below.

• Unstable carbonyls for the early members of transition series: For the early members of the transition series, the number of d-electrons is few (say 2, 3, etc.). To attain the 18e configuration, it needs a larger number of CO groups (i.e. requirement of higher co-ordination number) which is disfavoured due to steric grounds. This is why the carbonyls formed by the early members of the series are relatively unstable. For example, [Ti(CO)6], [V(CO)6] are unstable.

• Change of oxidation state: Sometimes, to maintain the 18e rule, the metal centre may experience an oxidation state change. For example, [V(CO)6] (17 valence electrons = 5 + 6 × 2) is not stable but [V(CO)6]− (satisfying the 18 rule) is stable. In the electron count, V− is considered to provide 6 valence electrons. Similarly, [Mn(CO)5] (17 electron) changes easily to [Mn(CO)5]− or [Mn+I(CO)5Cl] to satisfy the 18e rule.

• Mechanistic paths of ligand substitution reactions in carbonyls and organometallics: This can be understood in terms of the 18e rule.

• Polymerization by losing CO groups and producing M–M bonds: Sometimes, the mononuclear carbonyls obeying the 18e rule may also undergo polymerization through the releasing of CO groups and producing the M–M bonds. In such polynuclear carbonyls, both bridging and non-bridging CO groups may be present. It is illustrated for [Fe(CO)5] (18e = 8 + 5 × 2).

2[Fe(CO)5]  →  [Fe2(CO)9] + CO

3[Fe(CO)5]  →  [Fe3(CO)12] + 3CO

[Fe(CO)5]: 18e (= 8e + 5 × 2e)

[Fe2(CO)6(μ2–CO)3]: Fe: 8e; 3COt: 3 × 2e; 3COb: 3 × 1e; 1 Fe–Fe: 1e = 18e

[Fe3(CO)10(μ2–CO)2]: for Fe** (four terminal CO): Fe = 8e, 4COt = 4 × 2e, 2 Fe–Fe = 2 × 1e = 18e; for each Fe* (bridged pair): Fe = 8e, 3COt = 3 × 2e, 2COb = 2 × 1e, 2 Fe–Fe = 2 × 1e = 18e

Reason for the acidity order of carbonyl hydrides

The more CO groups on the conjugate base, the more the negative charge is delocalised by M → CO π* back-bonding, so the acid is stronger: H[V(CO)6] > H[Mn(CO)5] > H[Co(CO)4].

Chapter 6 — Metal Carbonyls, Phosphines, Organometallics and M–M Multiple Bonds

Bonding in metal carbonyl

CO – σ-donor and π-acceptor

σ-donor: OC σ⟶  MM ⇄ CO (σ – HOMO of CO donates; π* – LUMO of CO accepts)
π-acceptor: OC  ←  M (π*)

When a ligand donates its e− pair to the central metal or metal cation and simultaneously accepts e− from the metal in its vacant d orbital or ABMO, this phenomenon is called synergic bonding.

Synergic bonding in metal carbonyl (CO B.O. = 3)

M ⇄ C≡O

Due to synergic bond:

Bond lengthdecreaseincrease

Filling of e− in ABMO of CO reduces the bond order.

–ve O.S. ∝ extent of back bonding

∝ 1/(C–O B.O.)

∝ M–C B.O.

∝ 1/(C–O B.E.)

★★ Q. If C–O bond length in CO is 1.128 Å, the dC–O in Fe(CO)5 will be:

Mu bonds (μ-bond)

The σ-bonds are characterised by the presence of C_∞ symmetry (i.e. cylindrical symmetry) but the σ-bonds developed by the donation of the elongated π-electron cloud lack C_∞. Such bonds are formed in different alkene complexes, e.g. Zeise's salt, and this type of σ-bond is sometimes described as μ-bonds.

N2 vs CO and NO+ as ligand

The HOMO of N2 is a σ-BMO which cannot be used for σ-donation towards the metal centre. There may be only weak π-acceptance in the LUMO (π*) from the metal centre.

On the other hand, the isoelectronic species like CO, NO+ etc. can act as π-acid ligands because of their suitable HOMO (σ-donation) and LUMO (π-acceptance).

π-acid nature

NO+ > CS > CO > N≡N > CN−

NO+ – most EN

CS – S has vacant d orbital, it can accommodate extra e− density

−C≡O+ – due to ≡O+, CO is a better π-acid ligand than N2

Note – N≡C− > −C≡N (π-acid); −C≡N > N≡C− (better ligand) (left atom is always the donor)

π-acid: PF3 > PCl3 > PCl2Ph > PClPh2 > PPh3 > PMe3

π-acid: PR3 < PPh3 < P(OPh)3

Octet complete ⇒ check EN

π-acid: PF3 > PCl3 > P(OAr)3 > PAr3 > PRAr2 > PR2Ar > PR3 (PCl3 > P(OAr)3 decided by EN)

NO+ > PF3 > CO (NO+ – more EN): CO is a better ligand than any P donor ligand except PF3.

P(OAr)3 > P(OMe)3 > PNR3

• Whenever the R group becomes more electronegative, the orbital that the R fragment uses to bond to phosphorus becomes more stable (lower in energy).

• This implies that the σ* orbital of the P–R bond also becomes more stable.

• At the same time, the phosphorus contribution to σ* orbital increases, and so the size of the σ* lobe that points toward the metal increases.

• Both of these factors make the empty σ* more accessible for back donation.

• The final order of π-acid character (decreasing) is:

PF3 > CO > PCl3 > PCl2Ph > PClPh2 > PPh3 > PMe3

M(dyz) + P(σ*) = M–P π bond

• The empty P–R σ* orbital plays the role of acceptor in metal complexes of PR3.

• As the atom attached to the P atom becomes more electronegative, the empty P–X σ* orbital becomes more stable (lower in energy) making it a better acceptor of electron density from the metal centre.

Metal dz² ⟸ phosphine (σ bond, P sp lone pair)Metal dx²–y² ⟸ phosphine (σ bond)Metal dyz ⟹ phosphine σ* (σ*-back-donation)

• Occupation of the P–R σ* orbital by back donation from the metal also implies that the P–R bonds should lengthen slightly on binding.

• In practice, this is masked by a simultaneous shortening of the P–R bond due to donation of the P lone pair to the metal, and the consequent decrease in P(lone pair)–R(bonding pair) repulsions.

• Once again, as in the case of CO, the M–L π bond is made at the expense of a bond in the ligand, but this time it is a σ, not a π, bond.

Structures of metal carbonyls

1. Mononuclear metal carbonyls: The structure of mononuclear metal carbonyls is pretty simple and easy to visualize. This is definitely due to the presence of only one metal centre. The general examples of mononuclear metal carbonyls include tetrahedral Ni(CO)4 and Pd(CO)4; the trigonal bipyramidal case of Fe(CO)5, Ru(CO)5 and Os(CO)5; and the octahedral geometries of V(CO)6, Cr(CO)6, Mo(CO)6 and W(CO)6.

M(CO)4: M = Ni, Pd

M(CO)5: M = Fe, Ru, Os

M(CO)6: M = V, Cr, Mo, W

2. Binuclear metal carbonyls: The structure of binuclear metal carbonyls comprises two metal centres and involves either metal–metal bonds or bridging CO groups or both. For example, Co2(CO)8 is known to exist in two isomers. The first one has D3d symmetry with one metal–metal bond and zero bridging carbonyls; the second one is of C2v symmetry and has two bridging CO ligands along with one metal–metal bond. The structure of Fe2(CO)9 exists with D3h symmetry and contains three bridging CO ligands and six terminal CO groups attached. Furthermore, M2(CO)10 (M = Mn, Tc, Re) exists with D4d symmetry with one metal–metal bond and five CO ligands attached to each of the metal centres.

Co2(CO)8: unbridged isomer (D3d) and CO-bridged isomer (C2v)

Fe2(CO)9 (D3h)

M2(CO)10, M = Mn, Tc, Re (D4d)

3. Polynuclear metal carbonyls: The structures of the polynuclear metal carbonyls comprise three or more metal centres and involve all bridging, all terminal, or a mixture of the two types of CO groups. For example, the Ru3(CO)12 cluster has D3h symmetry and comprises an equilateral triangle of Ru centres, each of which has two axial and two equatorial CO ligands. Os3(CO)12 has the same structure, whereas Fe3(CO)12 is different, with two bridging CO ligands, resulting in C2v symmetry. M4(CO)12 (M = Co, Rh) consists of a tetrahedral M4 core, but the molecular symmetry is C3v. Three carbonyl ligands are bridging ligands and nine are terminal. However, Ir4(CO)12 has perfect Td symmetry with no bridging CO ligand groups. The Rh4 and Ir4 clusters are more thermally robust than the Co4 compound, reflecting the usual trend in the strengths of metal–metal bonds for second- and third-row metals vs those for the first-row metals. Furthermore, [Re4(CO)16]2− has D2h symmetry with no bridging carbonyl. The structures of Os4(CO)16, Os4(CO)15 and Os4(CO)14 are somewhat more complex because of non-rigidity. The tetranuclear Os4(CO)16 is analogous to cyclobutane with a puckered structure. X-ray diffraction analysis of Os4(CO)14 unveiled an irregular tetrahedral Os4 skeleton with four weakly semi-bridging CO groups and four different Os–Os bond lengths. The experimental structure of Os4(CO)15 was determined to have a planar butterfly-like geometry consisting of two triangles sharing an edge. The hexanuclear M6(CO)16 (M = Rh, Co) exists with an octahedral core with alternate faces participating in the bridging, i.e. with four triply bridged and twelve terminal carbonyls.

M3(CO)12, M = Os, Ru (no bridging CO)

Fe3(CO)12 (two bridging CO)

M6(CO)16 (M = Co, Rh): octahedral M6 core; each M carries two terminal CO (12 in all) and four alternate faces are capped by μ3-CO.

Bond order and bond length: worked questions

Q. Give the bond order of CO, NO+, NO, NO−, O2, O2−, O22−.

Ans. CO 3; NO+ 3; NO 2.5; NO− 2; O2 2; O2− 1.5; O22− 1.

Q. Arrange NO+, NO, NO− in increasing N–O bond length.

Ans. NO+ < NO < NO− (bond order 3 > 2.5 > 2).

Q. Arrange O2+, O2, O2−, O22− in increasing O–O bond length.

Ans. O2+ (bond order 2.5) < O2 (2) < O2− (1.5) < O22− (1).

Q. Arrange [Mn(CO)6]+, [Cr(CO)6], [V(CO)6]− in increasing C–O bond length.

Ans. [Mn(CO)6]+ < [Cr(CO)6] < [V(CO)6]−: the more negative the metal, the stronger the π-back-donation into CO π*, so C–O weakens and lengthens (ν(CO) falls in the same order reversed).

Q. Compare the M–C bond length with the C–O bond length when π-back-bonding increases.

Ans. M–C becomes shorter (partial double bond) and C–O becomes longer (bond order falls below 3).

Valence Bond Theory

(1) According to VBT, formation of co-ordination compounds can be explained by hybridization and overlapping.

Tetrahedral hybridisation: sp3 or d3s

Since the s-orbitals are totally symmetric, they will be transforming as the totally symmetric representation in all groups. In the Td point group, therefore, s-orbitals transform as A1 species. The px-, py- and pz-orbitals as well as the dxy-, dxz- and dyz-orbitals transform as T2 species. This may be listed as follows:

Symmetry speciesA1T2
Atomic orbitals coming under each symmetryspx, py, pz; dxy, dxz, dyz

The s-orbital has to definitely involve in the hybridization since there should be one orbital of symmetry A1. As T2 indicates a triply degenerate set of orbitals, either the px-, py-, pz-orbitals or the set of dxy-, dxz-, dyz-orbitals may involve in hybridization. Hence, a set of four tetrahedral hybrid orbitals may be formed from one s- and three p-orbitals or one s- and three d-orbitals. Note the three d-orbitals used for hybridization.

Group theory can only tell us which are the orbitals involved in a particular type of hybridization. It cannot give any idea regarding the energy of orbitals involved. We have to get this idea from elsewhere, say from quantum mechanics. From energy considerations, we can say that the s- and p-orbitals utilized for tetrahedral hybridization will be from the same main energy level and hence we denote the hybridization by sp3. However, the s- and d-orbitals for the tetrahedral hybridization cannot be from the same main shell since there will be an appreciable difference between the energies of s- and d-orbitals of the same shell. Moreover, there will be a set of three p-orbitals in between the s- and d-orbitals. But the energies of the ns-orbital and the (n – 1)d-orbitals will be comparable and hence they can undergo hybridization. This will be denoted by d3s. Thus tetrahedral hybridization can be sp3 or d3s. In some cases there may be an appropriate mixing among the p- and d-orbitals.

In the elements of the second period, the tetrahedral hybridization (as in CH4 or NH4+) will be definitely sp3 as d-orbitals are available only in the upper energy levels. In MnO4− and CrO42−, the type of hybridization is most probably d3s, in which 3d- and 4s-orbitals are used. Of course, we do not discard completely the possibility of some mixing among 3d- and 4p-orbitals.

Hybridization scheme in K2Cr2O7

The diamagnetic behaviour of potassium dichromate and its structure involving two CrO42− tetrahedra linked through an O-atom are well clear by the d3s hybridization scheme in each CrO42− unit shown below:

Cr: 3d5 4s1
O: 2s2 2p4 (each terminal O)
O−: 2s2 2p5 (the other O; in the second unit, the bridging O)
Cr in each CrO42− unit

Each Cr pairs its six electrons with O: two terminal O atoms form σ + π bonds (Cr=O), and one O− and the bridging O form σ bonds. Four σ + two π bonds, all electrons paired, so K2Cr2O7 is diamagnetic. The two CrO42− tetrahedra (I and II) share the bridging O atom.

Hybridization scheme in K2MnO4

The paramagnetic behaviour and tetrahedral structure (with four σ- and two π-bonds) of this compound are well clear by the d3s hybridization scheme shown below:

Mn: 3d5 4s1 4p1
O: 2s2 2p4 (two O atoms)
O−: 2s2 2p5 (two O− ions)
Mn in MnO42−

d3s hybridization scheme with four σ- and two π-bonds leading to the formation of K2MnO4; the unpaired electron makes it paramagnetic.

(6) Complexes with d10 metal ions

Failures of VBT

1. It does not give a satisfactory explanation about inner and outer orbital complexes.

2. VBT cannot explain distortion in Cu2+ complexes.

3. VBT cannot explain the field strength of ligands.

4. VBT cannot explain stability, magnetism and colour of complexes satisfactorily.

5. It cannot predict the geometry of C.N. = 4 exactly.

6. VBT cannot explain the spectral properties of complexes.

7. VBT cannot explain kinetic and thermodynamic properties.

8. It cannot explain excitation of (n – 1)d e− to form inner orbital complexes.

e.g. (1) Co(II) (d7 system): promotion of the 7th (n – 1)d e− to a higher energy level.

e.g. (2) Cu(II) (d9 system): promotion of an e− from 3d to 4p.

9. No explanation for spin isomerism.

10. Non-existence of many complexes: e.g. [Co(CN)6]4−, [Ni(CN)6]4−, [Cu(NH3)6]2+, [Pt(NH3)6]2+, etc. do not exist.

pz does not participate as it lies above the plane of the ion.

Other examples: [Cu(en)2]2+, [Cu(NH3)4]2+, [Cu(bpy)2]2+ are sp2d.

• (n – 1)d0−3 systems: Such systems can always produce inner orbital octahedral complexes.

• (n – 1)d8−10 systems: Such systems generally produce outer orbital octahedral complexes.

• d9 system: For inner orbital square planar complex formation, the 9th d-electron is to be promoted to some higher energy level to provide the vacant dx²–y² orbital for the hybridization.

Octahedral complexes in terms of VBT

(i) (n – 1)d0−3 systems: The required two d-orbitals, i.e. dx²–y² and dz², for the hybridization are always available from the (n – 1) shell without rearranging the electrons in the (n – 1)d level. Such systems always form octahedral complexes through d2sp3 hybridization (i.e. inner orbital octahedral complexes).

d0 (e.g. Al3+)
[Al(OH2)6]3+
d1 (e.g. Ti3+)
[Ti(OH2)6]3+, [TiF6]3−
d2 (e.g. V3+)
[V(OH2)6]3+
d3 (e.g. V2+, Cr3+, Mn4+)
[V(OH2)6]2+, [Cr(NH3)6]3+, [MnF6]2−

The electron pairs donated by the ligands (L) in the vacant hybrid orbitals are denoted by ××.

(ii) d4−6 systems: To utilize the (n – 1)dx²–y² and (n – 1)dz² in the hybridization scheme d2sp3 (i.e. inner orbital complex formation), it requires rearrangement of the electrons in the (n – 1)d level. If the electronic configuration in the (n – 1)d level is kept undisturbed, then the required dx²–y² and dz² orbitals for the hybridization purpose may be obtained from the n-shell. It will lead to sp3d2 hybridization (i.e. outer orbital complex formation). Thus, depending on the conditions, the d4−6 systems can generate either inner orbital or outer orbital octahedral complexes. These are illustrated in the following examples.

d4 (e.g. Cr2+, Mn3+)
[Cr(bpy)3]2+, [Mn(CN)6]3−
[Cr(OH2)6]2+

For the d2sp3 hybridization of the d4 electronic configuration, the electrons in the (n – 1)d level are rearranged through pairing. On the other hand, in the sp3d2 hybridization, the electron distribution pattern in the (n – 1)d level is kept unchanged. It is evident that whether the inner orbital or outer orbital complex will be formed for a particular metal ion depends on the nature of the ligand.

d5 (e.g. Mn2+, Fe3+)
[Mn(OH2)6]2+, [FeF6]3−, [Fe(OH2)6]3+
[Mn(CN)6]4−, [Fe(CN)6]3−

For the d5 electronic configuration, to use the two (n – 1)d orbitals in d2sp3 hybridization, five (n – 1)d electrons are to be accommodated in three (n – 1)d orbitals (i.e. dxy, dyz, dzx), giving rise to only one unpaired electron. If sp3d2 hybridization is carried out, the five (n – 1)d electrons remain unpaired as in the free ion.

d6 (e.g. Fe2+, Co3+, Ni4+)
[Fe(CN)6]4−, [Co(NH3)6]3+, [NiF6]2−
[Fe(OH2)6]2+

For the d6 electronic configuration, if d2sp3 hybridization is carried out, there will be no unpaired electron, i.e. six (n – 1)d electrons are paired up in three d-orbitals (i.e. dxy, dyz, dzx). On the other hand, if sp3d2 hybridization is carried out then four unpaired electrons will be present as in the free ion.

(iii) d7 system: To execute d2sp3 hybridization, there are only three (n – 1)d orbitals (i.e. dxy, dyz, dzx) available to accommodate the electrons. These three (n – 1)d orbitals can accommodate a maximum of six electrons and then the seventh (n – 1)d electron is to be promoted to some higher energy level. Pauling proposed that for inner orbital complexes like [NiF6]3−, [NiCl2(diars)2]+, where diars = ortho-C6H4(AsMe2)2, the seventh 3d electron is promoted to the 5s orbital. Without reorganizing the electron distribution in the (n – 1)d level, the d7 system can adopt sp3d2 hybridization. Thus, for the d7 system, both possibilities may exist depending on the conditions.

d7 (e.g. Co2+, Ni3+)
[NiCl2(diars)2]+, [NiF6]3−, [Co(NO2)6]4−
[Co(OH2)6]2+

(iv) d8−10 systems: In such cases, through the rearrangement of (n – 1)d electrons in the (n – 1)d level and excitation of (x – 6) (x = 8, 9, 10) electrons to some higher energy levels, two vacant (n – 1)d orbitals cannot be provided for the hybridization to produce the σ-bonds because the process becomes energetically unfavourable. Thus such systems fail to produce inner orbital octahedral complexes and they generally produce outer orbital octahedral complexes.

d8 (e.g. Ni2+, Cu3+)
[CuF6]3−, [Ni(OH2)6]2+, [Ni(NH3)6]2+
d9 (e.g. Cu2+): [Cu(OH2)6]2+
d10 (e.g. Cu+, Zn2+)
[Zn(OH2)6]2+, [Zn(NH3)6]2+

Square planar complexes in terms of VBT

If the square planar geometry is supposed to lie in the xy-plane, then the required orbitals for hybridization are dx²–y², s, px and py. Theoretically, the d0−4 systems can adopt dsp2 hybridization (i.e. inner orbital type complex) without any change of electronic configuration in the (n – 1)d level; the d5−8 systems can adopt dsp2 hybridization through the rearrangement of electrons in the (n – 1)d level; the d9 system can attain dsp2 hybridization through the pairing of eight (n – 1)d electrons in the (n – 1)d level and promotion of the ninth (n – 1)d electron to some higher energy level; the d9−10 systems can adopt sp2d hybridisation (i.e. outer orbital type complex) keeping the electron distribution pattern in the (n – 1)d level unchanged.

In reality, the square planar geometry is well characterized for the d8 and d9 systems.

d8 system (e.g. Ni2+, Pd2+, Pt2+, Cu3+, etc.): To provide the (n – 1)dx²–y² orbital in the required dsp2 hybridization, the eight (n – 1)d electrons are to be paired up in the remaining four (n – 1)d orbitals.

d8
[Pt(NH3)4]2+, [MX4]2−

(M = Ni, Pd, Pt; X− = halide, CN−; for Ni(II) only CN−. For Ni2+, (n – 1)d = 3d; for Pd2+, (n – 1)d = 4d and for Pt2+, (n – 1)d = 5d.) For Pd2+, Pt2+, other ligands like NH3, Cl−, etc. can also lead to the same result.

d9 system: The square planar complexes of Cu(II) like [Cu(NH3)4]2+, [Cu(bigH)2]2+, etc. are the representative examples in this category. To provide the (n – 1)dx²–y² orbital for dsp2 hybridization, it is required to promote the ninth 3d electron to some higher energy level. Pauling suggested the promotion of the ninth unpaired 3d electron to the 4p level.

d9 (e.g. Cu2+)
[Cu(NH3)4]2+, [Cu(bigH)2]2+

(cf. inner orbital octahedral complex formation by the d7 system, where the seventh (n – 1)d electron is also required to be promoted to some higher energy level.)

Tetrahedral complexes in terms of VBT

For tetrahedral complexes, the most common mode of hybridization is (n)s(n)p3, i.e. sp3 (s + px + py + pz). Thus it should not depend on the nature of the electronic configuration in the (n – 1)d level, i.e. all systems represented by (n – 1)d0−10 can adopt the tetrahedral geometry keeping the electron distribution pattern in the (n – 1)d level unchanged.

In reality, tetrahedral complexes are well documented for the d0 (e.g. [Be(OH2)4]2+), d1 (e.g. [TiCl4]−), d5 (e.g. [FeCl4]−, [MnCl4]2−), d7 (e.g. [CoCl4]2−), d8 (e.g. [NiCl4]2−), d9 (e.g. [CuCl4]2−), d10 (e.g. [ZnCl4]2−, [Ni(CO)4]) systems.

[TiCl4]−

[MnCl4]2−, [FeCl4]−

Conditions favouring outer and inner orbital complexes in terms of VBT

• Dependence on the nature of ligands: If strongly electronegative elements like F and O act as the ligating sites, then outer-orbital complexes (e.g. sp3d2) are favoured. Such strongly electronegative donor sites concentrate the bonding electrons (to be donated to the metal centre) near themselves. In other words, the bonding orbitals of such electronegative donor sites remain contracted. For the metal centres of, specially, the 3d-series, the higher d-orbitals, i.e. nd orbitals, compared to the (n – 1)d orbitals, having a larger radial extension in space, can still overlap appreciably with the contracted orbitals of the ligating sites. On the other hand, for the low electronegative donor sites like C, P, As, etc., having relatively more expanded (i.e. less contracted) donor orbitals, the lower d-orbitals, i.e. (n – 1)d orbitals, having a relatively smaller radial extension in space, are still efficient for effective overlapping. In such cases, metal–ligand π-bonding also becomes quite important.

Outer orbital complex:Contracted donor orbitals of the strongly electronegative donor atoms can overlap better with the expanded higher d-orbitals of the metal centre.
Inner orbital complex:Expanded donor orbitals of the relatively less electronegative donor atoms can overlap effectively even with the relatively contracted lower d-orbitals of the metal centre. In such cases, metal–ligand π-bonding may be quite important.

• Dependence on the periodic position of the metal ions: Generally, the heavier congeners, i.e. the members of the 2nd and 3rd transition series, prefer inner orbital complexes.

For the heavier congeners, compared to the lower d-orbitals, i.e. (n – 1)d orbitals, the higher d-orbitals, i.e. nd orbitals, are too diffused (cf. relativistic expansion of d-orbitals) to overlap effectively with the donor orbitals of the ligands. This is why the heavier congeners generally prefer the (n – 1)d orbitals for bonding, i.e. inner-orbital complexes (e.g. [Fe(OH2)6]3+ (outer orbital complex) vs. [Ru(OH2)6]3+ (inner orbital complex)).

• Dependence on the magnitude of positive charge on the metal centre: Increased positive charge on the metal centre prefers the participation of (n – 1)d orbitals compared to the nd orbitals. For a higher positive charge on the metal centre, the nd orbitals are too diffused compared to the (n – 1)d orbitals to overlap with the ligand orbitals. These are illustrated by the examples: [Co(NH3)6]2+ is an outer orbital complex while [Co(NH3)6]3+ is an inner orbital complex.

[MnF6]3−, [FeF6]3−, [CoF6]3− are outer orbital complexes (sp3d2) while [NiF6]2−, [PtF6]2−, etc. are inner orbital complexes (d2sp3).

Inner orbital complex formation at the cost of excitation of one unpaired electron

• Octahedral complexes of the d7 system (e.g. CoII, NiIII): It has already been discussed that in such cases, for the formation of inner orbital complexes (i.e. d2sp3 hybridization), the 7th (n – 1)d electron is to be promoted to some higher energy level like the 5s orbital.

d7 system
[CoIIL6]

For the excitation of the 7th electron to the higher energy level, some energy is required. This disfavour is compensated by the stronger bonding interaction provided by the (n – 1)d orbitals (compared to the nd orbitals). The excited electron at the higher energy level can be lost easily to favour the oxidation of Co(II) to Co(III). In fact, many Co(II) complexes are prone to oxidation to Co(III). However, this prediction cannot be generalized.

[CoIIL6] – e  →  [CoIIIL6] (favourable condition and experimentally realised)

• Octahedral complexes of the d8 system (e.g. NiII, CuIII): To execute the d2sp3 hybridization, two (n – 1)d electrons are to be promoted to some higher energy level (say the 5s orbital).

d8 system (e.g. NiII)
[NiIIL6]

For the excitation of two (n – 1)d electrons to the higher energy level, a large amount of energy is required. This high disfavour cannot be compensated by the favoured bonding interaction provided by inner orbital complex formation (i.e. d2sp3 hybridization). This is why such systems avoid d2sp3 hybridization and adopt sp3d2 hybridization, which does not require any excitation energy for the promotion of (n – 1)d electrons to the higher energy levels.

• Square planar complexes of the d9 system (e.g. CuII): If dsp2 hybridization, i.e. utilization of the (n – 1)dx²–y² orbital, is considered, then the ninth (n – 1)d electron is to be promoted to some higher energy level (say an np orbital).

d9 system (CuII)
[CuIIL4]

If it is argued that the excited electron will be lost easily, then it is reasonable to expect that square planar complexes of Cu(II) will be prone to oxidation to Cu(III) (cf. the ease of oxidation of octahedral CoII complexes having the d7 configuration). However, experimentally this prediction is not found true for Cu(II) square planar complexes.

[Cu(NH3)4]2+ – e  →  [Cu(NH3)4]3+ (not experimentally realised)

Note: In terms of magnetic properties, the dsp2, sp2d and sp3 (tetrahedral geometry) hybridization schemes for four-coordinate Cu(II) complexes cannot be distinguished. All three schemes keep coordination number four with one unpaired electron.

Hybridisation of some special complexes

• (NH4)2[CuCl4] and Cs2[CuCl4]: the geometry of [CuCl4]2− depends on the cation (crystal packing and hydrogen bonding): flattened towards square planar in the NH4+ salt and distorted tetrahedral in the Cs+ salt.

• [NiCl2(PMe3)2] (weak-field Cl−, strong-field PMe3): exists as an equilibrium between the square planar (dsp2, diamagnetic) and tetrahedral (sp3, paramagnetic) forms.

• Octahedral complexes of d0 to d3 ions (for example CrVI, d0, and CrIII, d3) are always inner-orbital d2sp3, whatever the ligand field, because the t2g set has empty orbitals available.

Chapter 8 — Crystal Field Theory, Jahn–Teller Effect and Spin-State Equilibrium

Crystal Field Theory (CFT)

CFT was developed by Hans Bethe and Van Vleck.

According to CFT,

(1) Ligands are point charges or point dipoles: point charges in the case of anions and dipoles in the case of neutral ligands.

(2) Wave mechanical identity of atomic orbitals of the metal centre: Though the ligands are considered as point negative charges, the metal e− are supposed to maintain their wave mechanical identity. In other words, the metal centre is supposed to bear the appropriate atomic orbitals to interact with the electrostatic field provided by the point-like negative charges, e.g. ligands.

(3) Metal–ligand interactions are basically electrostatic (ion–ion, ion–dipole). No covalent interaction.

(4) If an unsymmetrical field is generated, then the degeneracy of the d-orbitals is lost and they split into orbitals of different energy. Such splitting is known as crystal field splitting.

(5) C.F.T. explains back pairing (pairing) of e− in co-ordination compounds by the concept of crystal field stabilisation energy (CFSE) and pairing energy (PE).

(6) When CFSE > P.E., back pairing is observed.

(7) Colour of co-ordination compounds is explained by d–d transition. Complexes absorb light of suitable wavelength and show the complementary colour.

(8) CFT explains the relative strength of ligands on the basis of the spectrochemical series.

Shapes of d-orbitals

dxy, dyz, dzx: lobes between the axes; dx²–y²: lobes along the x and y axes; dz²: two lobes along z with a doughnut (torus) in the xy-plane.

Crystal field splitting in octahedral complex

In octahedral complexes, the nature of splitting can be obtained by viewing the formation of the complex as a two-step process:

1. In the first step, the ligands approach the central metal, producing a hypothetical field which repels all of the d-orbitals to the same extent.

Hollow sphere (spherical electrical field)

2. The ligands exert an octahedral field, which splits the orbitals' degeneracy.

Octahedral field: six ligands at the corners of an octahedron (at the face centres of a cube) around M.

Crystal field splitting of d-orbitals in an octahedral field.

Energy order: dx²–y² = dz² > dxy = dyz = dzx

Bary centre: It is the weighted mean of energy of the eg and t2g sets of orbitals.

Δo = 10 Dq (Dq: differential of quanta)

D = 35ze4a5    q = 2er4105    i.e. Dq = ze2r46a5

• a = distance of ligand from central atom

• r4 = fourth power of the radius of the d e− in the central atom

If the eg set is displaced upward by x from the pre-splitting barycentre, then the t2g set will move downward by y so that the following condition is maintained:

10E = 4(E + x) + 6(E – y)

2x = 3y

Here E denotes the energy of each electron prior to splitting. It leads to:

4x = 6y

Taking x + y = Δo = 10 Dq, we can write:

x + 2x3 = Δo ⟹ 5x3 = Δo
x = 35Δo    y = 25Δo

• t2g: triply degenerate; eg: evenly or doubly degenerate.

• g stands for gerade; g denotes the presence of a centre of symmetry.

Different conventions to express the CFSE

• The energy of an electron in the t2g level (of an octahedral system) is –4Dqo with respect to that of the barycentre and similarly, the energy of an electron in the eg level is +6Dqo with respect to that of the barycentre. The – sign (for the t2g level) signifies the stabilization. Thus it indicates that a t2g electron is stabilized by 4Dqo while an eg electron is destabilized by 6Dqo (measured with respect to that of the barycentre). Thus for the t2g3 eg1 configuration we can write:

t2g3 eg1: –3 × 4Dqo + 6Dqo = –6Dqo (crystal field energy with respect to that of the barycentre)

It means that the t2g3 eg1 configuration is stabilized by 6Dqo (with respect to the pre-splitting condition) due to crystal field splitting. Thus it is reasonable to say that the CFSE of the system is 6Dqo. However, many authors express the CFSE of the system as –6Dqo, i.e. the crystal field energy of the system is treated as the CFSE. It is not justified.

Thus the convention to be used to express the CFSE depends on the choice of the readers.

• Pairing energy (P) is to reduce the CFSE and this is why it is added with a negative sign with the CFSE (e.g. t2g4 eg0: CFSE = 4 × 4Dqo – P). However, in the alternative convention, the CFSE of the t2g4 eg0 system is given by: –4 × 4Dqo + P. It is not justified.

• Many authors do not include the pairing energy in expressing the CFSE. It is an approximation.

• If the pairing energy (P) is to be included in the CFSE, then the additional pairings, required compared to that of the pre-splitted condition, are to be considered. Obviously, the CFSE of a high spin complex (where no additional pairing is required compared to that in the free ion) does not contain any pairing energy term and the CFSE of a low spin complex (d4, d5, d6 and d7 systems) contains the additional pairing energy term.

But some authors consider the total number of pairings present in the splitted condition. For example, in the t2g6 eg0 configuration, though there are two additional pairings (i.e. 2P), some authors consider three pairings (i.e. 3P) in expressing the CFSE. However, it is not justified.

Conditions favouring the low-spin complex formation

The condition Δo > P is easily attained when the crystal field splitting is high and pairing energy is less.

(i) High positive charge on the metal centre and the strong field ligand produce a high Δo value to favour low-spin complex formation. Here it is worth mentioning that the higher positive charge on the metal centre slightly enhances the pairing energy to disfavour low spin complex formation. However, the relative effect on Δo is more than that on P. Thus, in general, the high oxidation state favours low spin complex formation.

(ii) Heavier congeners give a higher Δo value and lower pairing energy to favour the low-spin state.

(iii) The pairing energy runs as: d5 > d4 > d6 for a particular oxidation state. Thus spin pairing is easiest for the d6 system (e.g. Co(III)) while it is most difficult for the d5 system (e.g. Fe(III)). In fact, most Co(III) complexes are low-spin complexes.

(iv) Pi-acid ligands can favour formation of low-spin complexes in two ways: strong field character, and favouring electron pairing by reducing the electron–electron repulsion through metal → ligand π-back bonding.

Crystal field splitting in tetrahedral complex

In tetrahedral complexes, ligands approach the metal through planes (between the axes). As a result, the non-axial orbitals experience greater repulsion and they lose the degeneracy. It leads to splitting of the d-orbitals into two sets of new orbitals: e (eg) and t2 (t2g).

Note: No d-orbital points exactly towards the ligands in a tetrahedral complex, while dxy, dyz and dzx are nearer to the ligands than dx²–y² and dz². The splitting is small as compared to octahedral.

Energy order: dxy = dyz = dzx > dx²–y² = dz²

CFSE = (–35 × eg e– + 25 × t2g's e–)Δt = (–0.6 × eg e– + 0.4 × t2g's e–)Δt

In a tetrahedral field there is no centre of symmetry, so the sets are strictly labelled e and t2 (without g).

Crystal field splitting of the d-orbitals in a square planar crystal field

There are conceptually different approaches to understand the splitting of d-orbitals in a square planar crystal field. We can start with the square planar arrangement of the ligands along the ±x and ±y directions in the xy-plane. Through the compression of a tetrahedral geometry, the square planar geometry can be attained (i.e. Td → D2d → D4h). In terms of the other concept, to understand the crystal field splitting of the d-orbitals in a square planar crystal field, we can start with the octahedral crystal field.

(A) Octahedral ligand field → Square planar ligand field (i.e. Oh → D4h): If the two trans-axial ligands (say, along the ±z directions) of an octahedral geometry are taken to infinity, then the square planar crystal field is developed where the four ligands lie in the ±x and ±y directions. Removal of the ligands along the ±z directions from an octahedral geometry stabilizes (relatively) the orbitals having the z-components. Because, such orbitals will experience a less electrostatic repulsion from the ligands compared to the other orbitals.

In the square planar geometry (in the xy-plane), the ligands directly face the lobes of the dx²–y² orbital. Thus, the dx²–y² orbital will be destabilized maximum. The orbital dxy, lying in the xy-plane and projecting the lobes between the adjacent ligands, will be also destabilized next to the dx²–y² orbital. There is no electrostatic repulsive ligand field along the ±z directions and consequently, the dz² orbital is stabilized maximum though it has a small cocentric lobe in the xy-plane. The lobes of the dxz and dyz orbitals are not in the immediate vicinity of the ligands but they bear the x- and y-component respectively. Both of them also possess the z-component. The presence of the z-component stabilizes the orbitals but the presence of x- and y-components will destabilize these orbitals to some extent. In fact, the dxz and dyz orbitals are stabilized to some extent compared to the starting case of the octahedral geometry.

Note: this paragraph places dz² lowest, while the energy order above places dyz, dzx lowest. Both orders are reported; the relative position of dz² and (dxz, dyz) depends on the complex.

Macrocyclic effect:

(2) Charge on metal

CFSE ∝ charge of central metal

[Fe(CN)6]4− (EAN = 36) < [Fe(CN)6]3− (EAN = 35)

Note: Same metal, same ligands: Δo ∝ a−5; same number of ligands: Δo ∝ z (z = charge on ligand).

Oxidation state of the metal centre: With the increase of positive oxidation state of the metal centre, the electrostatic attraction between the ligand centre and metal centre increases. The ionic size of the metal centre also decreases with the increase of the positive oxidation state. Thus the increased electrostatic metal–ligand attraction and decreased ionic radius of the metal centre shortens the metal–ligand distance with the increase of positive charge of the metal centre. The shorter metal–ligand distance causes a better electrostatic effect to split the metal d-orbitals.

The magnitude of Δ is highly sensitive to the metal–ligand interacting distance (a) as follows:

Δo ∝ a−x, x = 5 – 6

Thus for the higher oxidation state, a decreases and consequently the splitting becomes higher. In fact, in moving from the +2 state to the +3 state, the crystal field splitting increases by ~50%.

Δ(M2+) : Δ(M3+) : Δ(M4+) ≈ 1 : 1.6 : 1.9 (ratio of the g values, i.e. Δ values)

(5) Exchange energy

The higher value of Δo prevents the exchange phenomenon between the t2g and eg sets. Thus to gain the stabilisation through the exchange energy, Δo is reduced (cf. d5 system of Mn2+).

Limitations of CFT

(1) CO is a stronger ligand than CN− while it is neutral. Many anions are at the lower end of the spectrochemical series while neutral ligands are at the higher end.

(2) CFT cannot account for the π-bonding in the complex.

(3) The radial wave functions of the d-orbital and of the ligand should have some overlap at the observed internuclear distance in a metal complex (i.e. bonding is not purely electrostatic).

(4) CFT cannot explain charge transfer spectra and the intensity of absorption bands.

Conditions favouring low spin complex formation

(1) High +ve charge on the metal centre

(2) Heavier congeners

(3) Pairing energy

(4) π-acid ligands

Critical crystal field strength (i.e. Δo ≈ P): spin-state equilibrium; temperature controlled spin isomerism

Variation of energy of high spin and low spin states with Δo for d4, d5, d6, d7 systems

• Low spin system: Δo > P; high spin system: Δo < P (for d4, d5, d6, d7 systems).

• Under the condition of the critical value of Δo, i.e. Δo = P, both H.S. and L.S. complexes have the same CFSE. This will lead to the spin equilibrium, i.e.

h.s.  ⇌  l.s. (for dn, n = 4, 5, 6, 7)

The critical value of Δo is described as the high-spin low-spin crossover point. If the crystal field strength lies close to the crossover region, then the spin state equilibrium is attained and it leads to anomalous magnetic moments.

If the energy difference between the two spin states is of the order of kBT (i.e. thermal energy) then the position of the equilibrium will depend on the temperature.
