The slopes of the two lines are different. As the Δo value increases, energies of both states (i.e. h.s. and l.s.) will decrease but the energy of the l.s. state will decrease more steeply. This can be rationalized by considering the energy of the two spin states.

It is evident that the energy of the low-spin state decreases more sharply compared to the corresponding high-spin state with the increase of ligand field strength. For the d4 system, for the plot of energy vs. Δo, the slope of the h.s. state is –3/5 while for the l.s. state it is –8/5. Similarly, for the plot of energy vs. Δo, the slopes are as follows:

Thus we can conclude: below the critical crystal field strength, the high-spin state is the ground state while above the critical crystal field strength, the low-spin state is the ground state.

Conversion of a h.s. state to a l.s. state leads to the transfer of one electron (for the d4 and d7 systems) or two electrons (for the d5 and d6 systems) from the eg orbitals, which directly face the ligands, to the

t2g level and it will shrink the metal–ligand bond distance (r). Thus the Δo value for the low-spin state is relatively higher (cf. Δo ∝ 1/rx, x = 5 – 6). Thus the l.s. state will have its minimum energy for the smaller r value compared to that for the h.s. state. The potential energy curves for the h.s. and l.s. states are shown below. For the crossover region, the minimum energies for the two curves are the same.

• Effect of temperature on the h.s.  ⇌  l.s. process: The origin of the thermally controlled spin crossover can be rationalized in terms of the potential wells of the two states. The metal–ligand bond distance in the low-spin state is relatively shorter than that in the high-spin state. The crossover point leading to the thermally controlled spin isomerism arises when the difference (ΔEo) in zero-point energies of the two states is of the order of kBT (i.e. thermal energy), i.e. ΔEo ≈ kBT. This condition is attained for 10Dqo ≈ P.

• Effect of pressure on the h.s.  ⇌  l.s. process: In the region of the crossover point, the position of the equilibrium may also depend on the external pressure that will try to reduce the volume. If the eg electrons (directly facing the approaching ligands) are shifted to the t2g level (i.e. change from the high-spin state to the low-spin state), then the molar volume of the complex will be reduced. Thus the external pressure will drive the equilibrium from the high-spin state to the low-spin state.

Potential energy curves for the high-spin and low-spin states at the crossover point. (Note: thermal spin cross-over under the condition ΔEo ≈ kBT.)

Examples experiencing h.s.  ⇌  l.s.

(i) Tris-dialkyldithiocarbamatoiron(III), i.e. [Fe(S2CNR2)3], shows the spin-state equilibrium in benzene solution in the monomeric form.

The magnetic moment (at room temperature) varies in the range μ = 5.80 – 3.0 B.M. depending on the nature of the alkyl group (R). At low temperature, the magnetic moment tends to 2.1 B.M. corresponding to t2g5 eg0 (i.e. low-spin state). With the increase of temperature, the observed magnetic moment gradually increases. The tris(dithiocarbamato)iron(III) complexes prefer to adopt the low-spin state at higher pressure because the transformation into the low-spin state reduces the molar volume.

Note: It has been already pointed out that the pairing energy (P) in the d5−systems (e.g. FeIII) is very high because of the loss of a huge amount of exchange energy on pairing the electrons. But in the presence of S-donor ligands, the pronounced nephelauxetic effect reduces the pairing energy (cf. participation of the vacant d-orbitals of sulfur in the metal → ligand π-bonding). In fact, in the present Fe(III) complex, the nephelauxetic effect helps to satisfy the condition Δo ≈ P.

(ii) [Fe(phen)2X2] (X = NCS, NCSe) also shows spin-state isomerism. The observed magnetic moment increases with the increase of temperature.

(iii) [Co(terpy)2]Cl2·3·5H2O also shows spin isomerism.

(iv) Bis-(2,6-pyridinedialdehydrazone)cobalt(II) iodide shows spin isomerism.

(Note: Many paramagnetic tetrahedral complexes of Ni(II) are converted into diamagnetic square planar complexes when pressure is increased. This actually represents conformation isomerism.

tetrahedral-Ni(II)  ⇌  square planar-Ni(II)

The above equilibrium is shifted to the right side with the increase of pressure. The paramagnetic tetrahedral complexes may be considered as the h.s. complexes and the diamagnetic square planar complexes may be considered as the l.s. complexes. The complex bis(N,N-diethylamino-troponeiminato)nickel(II) remains in such a pressure dependent equilibrium.)

Jahn–Teller theorem: Any non-linear molecular system in an orbitally degenerate electronic state would be unstable and it will get stabilized by undergoing distortion in its geometry and thus lower its symmetry and remove the degeneracy.

Chapter 9 — Isomerism in Coordination Compounds

Isomerism in coordination compounds

Isomerism in co-ordination complexes

• Structural isomerism: ionisation isomerism; hydrate isomerism; linkage isomerism; co-ordination isomerism; co-ordination position isomerism; ligand isomerism; polymerisation isomerism.

• Stereoisomerism: geometrical; optical.

(1) Ionisation isomerism

The compounds having the same M.F. but producing different types of ions in aq. solution are ionisation isomers.

[Co(NH3)5Br]SO4 (violet)  ⇌  [Co(NH3)5Br]2+ + SO42−

[Co(NH3)5SO4]Br (red)  ⇌  [Co(NH3)5SO4]+ + Br−

It occurs due to exchange of the ligating ion and the ions residing outside the co-ordination sphere.

(a) [CoClBr(NH3)4]NO2, [Co(NO2)Br(NH3)4]Cl, [Co(NO2)Cl(NH3)4]Br

(b) [PtCl2(en)2]Br2, [PtClBr(en)2]ClBr, [PtBr2(en)2]Cl2

They differ in molar conductance, colour, chemical tests, etc.

[CoBr(NH3)5]SO4  ⇌  [CoBr(NH3)5]2+ + SO42− (2–2 electrolyte) (violet)

[Co(NH3)5(SO4)]Br  ⇌  [Co(NH3)5(SO4)]+ + Br− (1–1 electrolyte) (red)

Preparation of the above violet and red isomers

CoBr2 O2 (air)⟶NH4Br + NH4OH [Co(NH3)5(OH2)]Br3 heating⟶  [CoBr(NH3)5]Br2

[CoBr(NH3)5]Br2 Ag2SO4⟶–2AgBr [CoBr(NH3)5]SO4 (violet)

[CoBr(NH3)5]SO4 (violet) conc. H2SO4⟶–Br2 [Co(NH3)5(SO4)]HSO4 (conc. H2SO4 oxidises Br− to Br2)

[Co(NH3)5(SO4)]HSO4 BaBr2⟶–BaSO4 [Co(NH3)5(SO4)]Br (red)

The molar conductance values of the violet isomer, pentaamminebromidocobalt(III) sulfate (2–2, i.e. bi-bivalent electrolyte) and the red isomer pentaamminesulfatocobalt(III) bromide (1–1, i.e. uni-univalent electrolyte) are different.

Violet compound (in solution) BaCl2⟶  white precipitate of BaSO4

Red compound (in solution) AgNO3⟶  pale yellow precipitate of AgBr

• The IR spectra of monodentately bound sulfate (in the red isomer) and free sulfate (in the violet isomer) are different.

Other sets of examples of ionisation isomerism are:

(i) [CoCl2(NH3)4]NO2 and [CoCl(NH3)4(NO2)]Cl; trans-[CoCl2(en)2]NO2 (green) and trans-[CoCl(en)2(NO2)]Cl (red)

(ii) [CoCl(en)2(NO2)]Br, [CoBr(en)2(NO2)]Cl and [CoBrCl(en)2]NO2

(iii) [CoCl2(NH3)4]NO2 and [CoCl(NH3)4(NO2)]Cl

(iv) [PtCl2(NH3)4]Br2, [PtBrCl(NH3)4]BrCl and [PtBr2(NH3)4]Cl2

Difference in the properties of ionisation isomers: The ionisation isomers differ in properties like colour, molar conductance, chemical tests for the respective ions, IR spectra, etc.

(2) Hydration or solvation isomerism

The compounds which have the same M.F. but differ in the number of water molecules present as ligands and the number of H2O molecules of hydration are called hydrate isomers.

CrCl3·6H2O: three isomers

(a) ★ [Cr(H2O)6]Cl3: violet; [Cr(H2O)5Cl]Cl2·H2O: green; [Cr(H2O)4Cl2]Cl·2H2O: dark green

[Cr(H2O)3Cl3]·3H2O is not taken in the isomers (not stable).

(b) [Cr(en)2(H2O)2]Br3 and [Cr(en)2(H2O)Br]Br2·H2O

(c) [CoCl2(NH3)4]Cl·H2O and [Co(H2O)Cl(NH3)4]Cl2

[Cr(H2O)6]Cl3violet(three ionic chlorines)
[Cr(H2O)5Cl]Cl2·H2Ogreen(two ionic chlorines)
[Cr(H2O)4Cl2]Cl·2H2Odark green(one ionic chlorine)

What is commercial CrCl3·6H2O? What is the colour of Cr2(SO4)3 solution?

Commercial CrCl3·6H2O is constituted by the above mentioned three isomers. The predominant form is trans-[CrCl2(OH2)4]Cl·2H2O. These isomers can be separated by using cation exchange resins followed by elution with dil. HClO4 of different concentrations. The green solution of commercial CrCl3·6H2O on standing for a prolonged period is gradually converted into a violet solution through aquation generating [Cr(OH2)6]Cl3.

The colour of chromic sulfate solution was only referred to elsewhere: freshly prepared cold solutions are violet ([Cr(OH2)6]3+); on heating they turn green as sulfate enters the coordination sphere.

(3) Linkage isomerism

It is due to the presence of an ambidentate ligand. In this isomerism, isomers differ in the mode of attachment of the ligand.

(a) NO2− and ONO−

[Co(NH3)5(ONO)]2+ (red) slow⟶heating [Co(NH3)5(NO2)]2+ (yellow)

(b) SCN− and NCS−

[Pd(bpy)(SCN)2] (orange yellow) 150 °C⟶in solid form [Pd(bpy)(NCS)2] (light yellow)

Many other linkage isomers involving the SCN− ligand are well known, e.g.

[Co(NH3)5(SCN)]2+  ⇌  [Co(NH3)5(NCS)]2+

[Rh(NH3)5(SCN)]2+  ⇌  [Rh(NH3)5(NCS)]2+

[Zn(SCN)4]2−  ⇌  [Zn(NCS)4]2−

[Co(SCN)4]2−  ⇌  [Co(NCS)4]2−

[Hg(SCN)4]2−  ⇌  [Hg(NCS)4]2−

[Pd(SCN)4]2−  ⇌  [Pd(NCS)4]2−

[Cd(SCN)4]2−  ⇌  [Cd(NCS)4]2−

The relative stability of the above mentioned linkage isomers can be explained by considering the matching of hard–soft character and symbiotic effect.

(c) CN and NC: [Co(CN)2(trien)]+ and [Co(NC)2(trien)]+

(d) S2O32−:

• [(H3N)5Co–O–S2O2]+ and [(H3N)5Co–S–SO3]+

• [(NC)5Co–O–S2O2]4− and [(NC)5Co–S–SO3]4−

Factors affecting relative stabilities of the linkage isomers

(i) HSAB principle

(ii) Symbiotic effect

(iii) Steric factors

(iv) π-bonding properties of ligand

(v) CFSE consideration

A. Hard–soft character matching and symbiotic effect: If other factors are less important then the HSAB principle works well, i.e. soft metal centres prefer the soft donor sites and hard metal centres prefer the hard donor sites. In terms of symbiosis, like ligands prefer the like ligands, i.e. hard and soft ligands prefer to group together separately.

This is why the soft metal centres like Hg(II), Pd(II), Pt(II), etc. prefer to bind with the S-end of SCN− and the Se-end of SeCN−, while the relatively harder sites like Co(II), Cr(III), Fe(III), Co(III), etc. prefer to bind the N-end of SCN− or SeCN−. It explains the following stability orders.

HSAB principle:

• [M(SCN)4]2− > [M(NCS)4]2− (M = Hg, Pd, Pt)

• [M(SeCN)4]2− > [M(NCSe)4]2− (M = Hg, Pd, Pt)

• [Hg(SCN)4]2− > [Cd(SCN)4]2− > [Zn(SCN)4]2−

• [Co(NCS)4]2− > [Co(SCN)4]2−

• [Cr(OH2)5(SCN)]2+ < [Cr(NCS)(OH2)5]2+

• cis-[M(NH3)2(SCN)2] > cis-[M(NCS)2(NH3)2] (M = Pt, Pd)

Symbiotic principle:

• [Co(NH3)5(NO2)]2+ > [Co(NH3)5(ONO)]2+

• [Co(CN)5(NCS)]3− < [Co(CN)5(SCN)]3−

• [M(NCS)(NH3)5]2+ > [M(NH3)5(SCN)]2+ (M = Co, Rh)

• [Co(CN)5(NC)]3− < [Co(CN)6]3−

• [Rh(SCN)6]3− > [Rh(NCS)(SCN)5]3−

• [Fe(CO)2(Cp)(SeCN)] > [Fe(CO)2(Cp)(NCSe)]

The FeII centre prefers the harder N-donor site of SeCN− as in [Fe(NCSe)4]2−, but when softened by Cp− and CO, it prefers to bind through the softer end of SeCN− as in [Fe(CO)2(Cp)(SeCN)]. Cp− and CO, being enriched with the π-electron cloud, can act as soft ligands.

It is evident from the above examples that in terms of the symbiotic principle, irrespective of the hardness of the metal centre, the harder ligands group together and similarly the softer ligands group together. Thus [Rh(SCN)6]3−, [Fe(NCSe)4]2−, etc. are stable.

B. Effect of π-bonding and competitive π-bonding interaction in square planar complexes: In the octahedral complex, the π-bonding effect is relatively less pronounced than that in the square planar complex. This is why the simple prediction of the HSAB principle or symbiotic principle may not always work in square planar complexes. This is illustrated (in terms of the stability order) in some representative examples of square planar complexes.

• cis-[Pt(NH3)2(SCN)2] > cis-[Pt(NCS)2(NH3)2] (contradicting the symbiotic principle) (S-bonded SCN− is a π-bonding ligand while N-bonded SCN− and NH3 are non-π-bonding ligands)

• cis-[Pt(NCS)2(PR3)2] > cis-[Pt(PR3)2(SCN)2] (contradicting the HSAB principle) (PR3 is a better π-bonding ligand than the S-bonded SCN− ligand)

• [Pd(SCN)4]2− > [Pd(NCS)4]2− (as expected from the HSAB principle) (S-bonded SCN− is a π-bonding ligand, but N-bonded SCN is a non-π-bonding ligand)

• [Pd(bpy)(NCS)2] > [Pd(bpy)(SCN)2] (contradicting the HSAB principle) (bpy is a better π-bonding ligand than the S-bonded SCN− ligand)

• cis-[Pd(NCS)2(XPh3)2] > cis-[Pd(SCN)2(XPh3)2] (contradicting the HSAB principle) (X = As, P) (XPh3 is a better π-bonding ligand than the S-bonded SCN ligand)

• trans-[Pd(PPh3)2(SCN)2] > trans-[Pd(NCS)2(PPh3)2] (as expected from the HSAB principle) (S-bonded SCN− as a π-bonding ligand does not compete with the better π-bonding ligand PPh3)

• Similarly, trans-[Rh(PPh3)2(SeCN)2]− > trans-[Rh(NCSe)2(PPh3)2]−

• trans-[Rh(CO)(NCSe)(PPh3)2] > trans-[Rh(CO)(PPh3)2(SeCN)] (CO and SeCN− at the trans-positions; CO is a better π-bonding ligand than the Se-bonded SeCN−)

When SCN− and SeCN− bind with their soft ends, i.e. the S-end and Se-end respectively, they can act as π-acceptor ligands. This π-bonding (metal to ligand) enhances the metal–ligand bonding interaction and thus the stability of the system increases. In the square planar complexes of the specially soft metal …

(iii) Linkage isomers from the ambidentate ligand CN−

CN− can bind through the C-end or N-end to produce linkage isomers.

• The prussian blue and related compounds are the classical examples. In prussian blue, the stable form possesses the following type of linkage:

Preference for the C-end (strong field ligand site) of CN− by the Fe(II) centre (d6) can be explained by considering the gain of CFSE.

• A similar linkage isomerism in the polymeric compound having the metal centres Fe(II) and Cr(III) connected by the bridging ligand CN− has been characterised.

FeSO4 + K3[Cr(CN)6] cold condition⟶(–K2SO4) KFeIICrIII(CN)6 (brick red solid)

KFeIICrIII(CN)6 (brick red) heating⟶(~100 °C) KCrIIIFeII(CN)6 (dark green)

Both the brick red and dark green solids have a polymeric structure similar to the skeleton structure of prussian blue. In the brick red solid (kinetically controlled product), the strong field donor ends (i.e. C-ends) of the CN− ligands octahedrally coordinate the CrIII centre (d3 system), while in the dark green solid (thermodynamically controlled product), the FeII centre (d6 system) is octahedrally coordinated by the C-ends of the CN− ligands.

Brick red (high spin FeII, N-bonded)

heating⟶ 

Dark green (low spin FeII, C-bonded)

In both forms, CrIII remains as t2g3, but FeII attains the low-spin state (t2g6 eg0) in the dark green product due to ligation by the strong field donor sites (i.e. C-ends) of the CN ligands, while FeII remains in the high-spin state (t2g4 eg2) in the brick red compound due to ligation by the weak field donor sites (i.e. N-ends). Thus the gain of CFSE makes the green product thermodynamically more stable.

Chapter 10 — Colour, Electronic Spectra, Charge Transfer and Selection Rules

Colour of complexes

Colour arises from: (1) d–d transition; (2) charge transfer; (3) crystal defect.

(1) d–d transition

Degeneracy of the five d-orbitals is lost in the ligand field. The colour of co-ordination compounds can be explained in terms of CFT.

e.g. [Ti(H2O)6]3+, which is violet in colour:

t2g1 eg0 hν (498 nm)⟶  t2g0 eg1 (d–d transition)

A certain component of white light is absorbed; the rest is reflected (transmitted). As a result, the e− of t2g is excited to eg.

In general, the stronger the ligand, the higher the value of Δo and the shorter the λabs; the weaker the ligand, the longer will be λabs.

Colour does not depend on the energy given but on the colour absorbed. In a solid lattice, there is an absorption spectrum, not an emission spectrum.

In atomic spectra, from a single atom the emitted energy is not dissipated; that's why an emission spectrum is observed.

Colour absorbedColour observed
Yellow–greenRed–violet
YellowIndigo

IndigoYellow

Blue–greenRed

Excitation of an e− from a lower energy d-orbital to a higher energy d-orbital in the presence of a ligand field is called d–d transition.

Conditions for d–d transition

1. There should be some ligand field around the central metal ion so that the degeneracy of the five d-orbitals is lost. (No p–p transition, as p-orbitals are axially symmetrical.)

2. Partially filled d-orbitals: A central metal ion having a d0/d10 configuration forms colourless compounds (white), whereas a central metal ion having a d5 configuration forms colourless complexes with hard donors (e.g. F−, OH−, etc.): [FeF6]3− is white whereas Fe(SCN)3 is blood red due to charge transfer and not d–d transition.

AgI (yellow) and Cu2O (red) are coloured due to charge transfer from I− to Ag+ and from O2− to Cu+.

HOMO–LUMO gap ↓ as covalency ↑, and it falls in the visible spectrum.

(2) Charge transfer

In a redox reaction, permanent transfer of e− (charge) takes place:

CuI2  →  CuI + 1/2 I2

Cu(CN)2  →  CuCN + 1/2 (CN)2

Cu(SCN)2  →  CuSCN + 1/2 (SCN)2

Temporary transfer of charge from an orbital localised on an atom or group to another orbital localised on another atom/group in a species leads to charge transfer spectra.

Intensity of colour due to charge transfer

Colour originates from one part of the complex to another part; such types of transition are called internal redox reactions. The intensity of colour in such transitions is very high as they do not need to follow the selection rule.

Examples of charge transfer:

(i) Charge transfer from ligand to metal (LMCT)

LMCT takes place when the central metal ion is present in its higher oxidation state or the complex contains soft ligands. This is also called a temporary reduction band.

MnO4−MnO42−CrO42−Cr2O72−CrO2Cl2
pink (purple)greenyelloworangered-brown

[Fe(SCN)3(H2O)3]: blood red; charge transfer is preferred over d–d transition.

LMCT is also known as CTTM (charge transfer to metal).

Electrons can be excited not only from t2g to eg orbitals, but also from σ-orbitals originating from ligands to eg orbitals.

(ii) Charge transfer from metal to ligand (MLCT)

MLCT or CTTL: this type of charge transfer takes place in coordination complexes having π-acceptor ligands. In these cases, empty π* orbitals on the ligands become the acceptor orbitals on absorption of light. Since the metal ion is temporarily oxidized, it is also known as a temporary oxidation band.

e.g. NO+, CN−, CO, SCN−, bipy, etc.

e.g. [Fe(CO)5], [Fe(π–C5H5)2], [Cr(π–C6H6)2]

★ MLCT is favoured by SFL (π-acceptor) and a low O.S. of the metal.

(iii) Charge transfer from metal to metal (MMCT)

This is observed when two metal ions in different O.S. are present in the co-ordination sphere.

Selection rules

• Orbital selection rule: Δl = ±1

• Spin selection rule: ΔS = 0

• Laporte allowed transitions: g → u, u → g

• Laporte forbidden transitions: g → g, u → u

Spin forbidden:

• [FeF6]3−: colourless

• [Mn(H2O)6]2+: very light pink, colourless when diluted

These are due to forbidden spin and orbital (Laporte) transitions.

Electronic transitions between energy levels obey the following selection rules:

Selection rules

Intensities of absorption bands of complexes: The electronic transitions between d-orbitals, i.e. t2g to eg in octahedral complexes or e to t2 in tetrahedral complexes, are called d–d transitions. When d–d transitions occur in complexes with centres of symmetry, such as regular octahedral complexes, the intensities of absorption bands are low. But when d–d transitions occur in complexes which lack centres of symmetry, such as tetrahedral complexes and octahedral cis-complexes of the type MA4B2, relatively strong absorption bands are observed. For example, when conc. HCl is added to an aqueous solution of Co(II), the colour changes from pink [Co(H2O)6]2+ to the intense blue colour of [CoCl4]2−.

The variation in the relative intensities of absorption bands can be explained by a series of selection rules.

(1) Laporte's selection rule

The transitions that occur between states of opposite parity, i.e. g ↔ u, are allowed. It means that s ↔ p, p ↔ d and d ↔ f transitions are allowed.

The transitions that occur between states of the same parity, i.e. g ↔ g or u ↔ u, are forbidden.

For example, d–d transitions are forbidden because d-orbitals are gerade, i.e. these have a centre of symmetry with respect to the wave function.

Laporte's selection rule may also be given as follows. The transitions in which the change in azimuthal quantum number is ±1, i.e. Δl = ±1, are Laporte allowed and the absorbance may be high. If Δl = 0, the transitions are Laporte forbidden and therefore the absorbance is low.

Relaxation in Laporte's selection rule

The d–d transitions are Laporte forbidden and, however, have much lower absorbance in the range of 10–50 L mol−1 cm−1 because there is slight relaxation in Laporte's selection rule. The metal–ligand bonds in transition metal complexes are not rigid. When UV-visible light is incident on a complex, electronic transitions as well as vibrations occur simultaneously. In octahedral complexes the ligands vibrate in such a way that the centre of symmetry is temporarily destroyed and there is a very small mixing of p–d orbitals, and thus d–d transitions are not purely Laporte forbidden but there is slight relaxation in Laporte's rule. Therefore, octahedral complexes show colour of low intensity.

In tetrahedral complexes there is no centre of symmetry and p–d mixing is more pronounced in tetrahedral complexes because t_2 molecular orbitals are formed from atomic d (gerade) and p (ungerade) orbitals. Tetrahedral complexes, therefore, absorb more strongly than octahedral complexes. Therefore, tetrahedral complexes give more intense colour than octahedral complexes.

(2) Spin selection rule

Transitions between states of the same multiplicity are allowed, i.e. ΔS = 0: spin allowed.

In other words, during an electronic transition, if the spin of the electron is not changed, then the transition is spin allowed.

Transitions between states of different multiplicities are spin forbidden, i.e. ΔS ≠ 0: spin forbidden.

For example: For the d2 configuration in an octahedral field, there are four states with the same spin multiplicity of 3 (S = 1), one of which is the ground state (³T1g) and the other three are excited states (³T2g, ³A2g and ³T1g(P)). Thus there are three transitions which are spin allowed. These are:

³T2g  ←  ³T1g

³A2g  ←  ³T1g

³T1g(P)  ←  ³T1g

The transitions from ³T1g to any other excited states are spin forbidden.

Relaxation in spin selection rule

Spin–orbit coupling can relax the spin selection rule, with the result that transitions may be observed from a ground state of one spin multiplicity to an excited state of different spin multiplicity. These spin-forbidden transitions are generally much weaker than spin allowed transitions. The strength of spin–orbit coupling in lighter atoms is lower than for heavier atoms. The intensity of such bands increases with increase in atomic number. In first series transition metal complexes, spin–orbit coupling is weak and, therefore, the absorption bands are weak with a molar absorptivity of about 1 L mol−1 cm−1. Spin–orbit coupling in 4d- and 5d-transition metal complexes is strong; absorption bands, therefore, are stronger, i.e. intensities of these complexes are greater than for 3d-metal complexes.

A Laporte forbidden d–d transition is more intense than a spin forbidden transition.

Practice questions

The marked answer of each question is given as Ans. All marked answers were checked.

Q. The light pink colour of [Co(H2O)6]2+ and the deep blue colour of [CoCl4]2− are due to

(a) MLCT transition in the first and d–d transition in the second

(b) d–d transition in both

(c) LMCT transition in both

(d) d–d transition in the first and MLCT transition in the second

Ans. (b)

Q. For the complex ion [Cu(NH3)6]2+, the number of possible d–d transitions will be

(a) one (b) two (c) three (d) four

Ans. (a)

Q. The compound which shows MLCT is

(a) K2Cr2O7 (b) Ni(CO)4 (c) HgO (d) [Ni(H2O)6]2+

Ans. (b)

Q. The complex [Mn(H2O)6]2+ has a very light pink colour. The best reason for it is

(a) presence of a ²T2g ground state and the complex does not have a charge transfer transition

(b) presence of a ²T2g ground state and d–d transitions here are orbital forbidden but spin allowed

(c) presence of a ⁶A1g ground state and d–d transitions here are orbital allowed but spin forbidden

(d) presence of a ⁶A1g ground state and d–d transitions here are both orbital and spin forbidden

Ans. (d)

(b) Colour changes with the strength of the ligand attached.

(c) If the compound absorbs violet light it will appear yellow.

(d) Colour of the complex depends upon crystal field stabilization energy.

Worked example

Results of a pH study using a glass electrode (in 2 M NH4NO3 aqueous solution) give values of the stepwise stability constants (at 303 K) of [Ni(OH2)6–x(NH3)x]2+ (x = 1–6) as: log K1 = 2.79; log K2 = 2.26; log K3 = 1.69; log K4 = 1.25; log K5 = 0.74; log K6 = 0.03. Calculate (a) β6 for [Ni(NH3)6]2+ and (b) ΔG°1(303 K). (c) If the value of ΔH°1(303 K) = –16.8 kJ mol−1, calculate ΔS°1(303 K). (R = 8.314 J K−1 mol−1)

(a) β6 = K1 × K2 × K3 × K4 × K5 × K6

log β6 = log K1 + log K2 + log K3 + log K4 + log K5 + log K6

log β6 = 2.79 + 2.26 + 1.69 + 1.25 + 0.74 + 0.03 = 8.76

β6 = 5.75 × 108

(b) ΔG°1(303 K) refers to the stepwise formation of [Ni(OH2)5(NH3)]2+.

ΔG°1(303 K) = –RT ln K1 = –(8.314 × 10−3 × 303) ln 102.79 = –16.2 kJ mol−1

(c) ΔG°1 = ΔH°1 – TΔS°1

ΔS°1 = ΔH°1 – ΔG°1T = –16.8 – (–16.2)303 = –1.98 × 10–3 kJ K–1 mol–1 = –1.98 J K–1 mol–1
